When Wannier centers jump: Critical points between atomic insulating phases

Yunchao Zhang Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge MA 02139-4307, USA    T. Senthil Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge MA 02139-4307, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We study a class of quantum phase transitions between featureless bosonic atomic insulators in (2+1)(2+1) dimensions, where each phase exhibits neither topological order nor protected edge modes. Despite their lack of topology, these insulators may be “obstructed” in the sense that their Wannier centers are not pinned to the physical atomic sites. These insulators represent distinct phases, as no symmetry-preserving adiabatic path connects them. Surprisingly, we find that for certain lattices, the critical point between these insulators can host a conformally invariant state described by quantum electrodynamics in (2+1)(2+1) dimensions (QED3). The emergent electrodynamics at the critical point can be stabilized if the embedding of the microscopic lattice symmetries suppresses the proliferation of monopoles, suggesting that even transitions between trivial phases can harbor rich and unexpected physics. We analyze the mechanism behind this phenomenon, discuss its stability against perturbations, and explore the embedding of lattice symmetries into the continuum through anomaly matching. In all the models we analyze, we confirm that the QED3 is indeed emergeable, in the sense that it is realizable from a local lattice Hamiltonian.

I Introduction

Atomic insulators are typically regarded as the most mundane of quantum phases; such systems are gapped to all excitations, and they lack topological invariants, protected edge modes, or any form of long-range entanglement. Furthermore, their ground states, by definition, can be adiabatically deformed into trivial product states without closing the bulk gap. However, a large body of work has revealed a subtle distinction within this class; while some atomic insulators are trivial in the strictest sense (admitting symmetric, exponentially localized Wannier functions centered at lattice sites), others are “obstructed” [12, 48, 37, 13, 71]. The obstructed atomic insulators are distinguished from the trivial class in that their Wannier centers lie away from the physical lattice sites.

Classes of obstructed atomic insulators (OAIs) have been studied as examples of higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) [5, 6, 53], where their non-triviality manifests when the system is terminated with boundaries. Unlike symmetry protected topological phases, which host anomalous gapless surface states, OAIs host surface states of lower dimensionality, such as gapless corner modes on a (2+1)(2+1) dimensional lattice.

However, even in the bulk, OAIs are distinct from trivial insulators. While obstructed atomic insulators preserve all symmetries of the lattice space group, they admit no smooth deformation to an on-site atomic limit without breaking symmetries.

We emphasize that the notion of which phase is trivial and which is obstructed is only a relative concept. This is because one must make an arbitrary choice, such as where to place the lattice sites or how to cut the boundary in a finite system, in order to designate a phase as the trivial phase [46, 12]. One example of this is in the Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) chain [61], in which the two phases have different polarization values that can be distinguished only relative to each other 11 1 This relative nontriviality is sometimes presented as an absolute one, but any such distinction requires fixing a convention for the unit cell or equivalently, fixing the locations of a background of positive ions. Mathematically, these relative topological distinctions are captured by the mathematical structure of a torsor, not a group or cohomology ring as is usual for the study of topological phases..

This raises a natural question: What can happen at a quantum phase transition between two such “trivial” insulating phases? To this end, we will consider critical points between atomic insulators in (2+1)​d(2+1)d. A simple example can be realized on the square lattice [5, 6] with multiple orbitals per site, in which one can tune a phase transition between two insulating states; one phase with localized atomic orbitals that sit on the atomic sites and another phase where the orbitals are centered at each plaquette, as shown in Fig. 1. In this case, at a filling of n≠0(mod4)n\neq 0\pmod{4} particles per unit cell, there is no C4C_{4} preserving deformation between the two phases. Therefore, there must be a transition between the two insulating phases.

Despite taking place between two trivial phases, there is no order parameter description of the phase transition. While two phases with the same microscopic symmetry can, in principle, be separated by a Landau-Ginzburg transition with an emergent scalar order parameter (as in the liquid-gas critical point, where the coarse-grained density is described by a single Ising order parameter), the exotic critical points we explore are not in the universality class of any Landau-Ginzburg theory. Instead, the closing of the single particle gap leads to a metallic critical point described by an interacting gauge theory. In fact, examples such as deconfined quantum critical points [65, 56] have illustrated that even transitions between conventional ordered phases can be beyond the Landau paradigm [57, 55].

In this paper, we show that a similar phenomenon occurs between featureless insulators, in which the insulating phases neither break symmetry nor carry topological order.

We observe that this already is realized for the quantum critical point between the two phases of the one-dimensional SSH chain in the presence of interactions. For both the bosonic and fermionic SSH chains, the quantum critical point realizes a Luttinger liquid, without quasiparticles.

Going to higher dimension, at the transition between two atomic insulators of bosons in (2+1)(2+1) dimensions, we find critical points described by Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3, a theory of 44 massless Dirac fermions coupled to an emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field. This theory has previously appeared as an effective description of quantum phases of matter such as algebraic spin liquids [52, 31, 27, 32, 33, 51, 30], which can arise as ground states of frustrated magnets. QED3 can also arise as an “unnecessary” quantum critical point within lattice magnets [74, 75]. Moreover, many magnetically ordered states can be obtained by tuning away from a lattice QED3 critical point [60]. From analytic and numerical calculations [3, 16, 38, 2, 29, 39], QED3 is believed to be a conformal field theory (CFT) in the IR. Therefore, in contrast to the theory of deconfined criticality [56], in which later work showed that the putative field theory of the transition was weakly first order and discontinuous [44, 43], the existing evidence for the conformality of Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 is very well established.

The stability of the QED3 critical point and consequently, the exact nature of the phase transition, is chiefly governed by how the microscopic (UV) lattice symmetries embed into the emergent continuum (IR) symmetries of the quantum critical theory [59, 60, 74]. At the lattice level, space group symmetries such as discrete translations, rotations, and discrete symmetries such as time reversal impose stringent conditions on which operators can be realized in the low energy effective theory. Even independent of the microscopic theory, the embedding of UV symmetries into the IR theory is subject to constraints from the ’t Hooft anomalies of the UV theory, which arise from the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis-Oshikawa-Hastings (LSMOH) theorems [40, 45, 28].

If the symmetry embedding in the IR permits no relevant operators other than the single one needed to tune to the critical point, then QED3 can emerge as a stable fixed point that describes a continuous transition between the two insulating phases. However, if lattice symmetries are insufficient to protect the critical theory and a relevant monopole perturbation is allowed, then the QED3 theory will confine, and the phase transition will generically become first-order.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. As a warm-up to our study of atomic insulator transitions, we begin in Sec. II by reviewing the paradigmatic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model [61], both in its fermionic and bosonic forms. This simple one-dimensional model exemplifies how obstructed atomic insulators, though topologically trivial in the absence of symmetry protection, can host distinct phases separated by a critical point and illustrates the key features that will be present in the two-dimensional models. In the fermionic case, the transition involves a Dirac fermion gaining mass, while the bosonic version, analyzed via both exact methods and a parton construction, introduces an emergent gauge field relative to the fermionic case. In both cases, the phase transition can be described by Luttinger liquid theory.

In Sec. III, we generalize the SSH model to two dimensions by analyzing models of atomic insulators on various lattices, such as the Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes (BBH) model [5, 6] on the square lattice. Like the SSH model, each fermionic atomic insulator features Dirac band touchings at the transition. For the bosonic analog, we employ a parton construction that fractionalizes the boson into two fermions coupled to an emergent gauge field, yielding a critical theory described by Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3. However, the intrinsic bipartiteness of the square and honeycomb lattices introduces a single symmetry-allowed monopole operator that destabilizes the fixed point. Together with a symmetry-allowed mass that tunes the transition, this drives the theory toward confinement and produces a highly multicritical point; we argue the transition is generically first-order. Key to our argument is the observation made in [59] that on a bipartite lattice, Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 admits a deformation to Nf=2N_{f}=2 QCD3, from which one can argue there is always at least one monopole operator that is a singlet under all UV symmetries.

In contrast, the C3C_{3} symmetric breathing kagome lattice is tripartite, and we demonstrate that monopoles are symmetry-disallowed, making QED3 a natural candidate universality class for a direct continuous transition. This highlights the strong dependence of criticality in trivial insulator transitions on the underlying (UV) lattice structure.

In Sec. IV, we employ anomaly matching arguments to support our analysis of the critical theories. By matching the LSMOH anomalies for lattice bosons in the IR [76, 72], we confirm that all discussed critical theories, even the unstable ones, are realizable by local lattice Hamiltonians. This establishes a rigorous link between the microscopic theory and emergent QED3 critical point. We conclude in Sec. V with broader implications and comments on extensions to three dimensional obstructed atomic insulators.

II A warm-up in one dimension: The SSH chain

II.1 Fermionic

A minimal model to illustrate the general case is the SSH model [61] in one dimension, which describes a chain with alternating bonds of two types between atoms, as in polyacetylene. The fermionic SSH chain has a tight binding Hamiltonian

HS​S​H=∑n=1N(t​cA,n†​cB,n+λ​cB,n†​cA,n+1)+h.c.,H_{SSH}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(tc_{A,n}^{\dagger}c_{B,n}+\lambda c_{B,n}^{\dagger}c_{A,n+1}\right)+h.c., (1)

which describes electrons hopping on a dimerized chain (with sublattice sites AA and BB) at half filling. Equivalently, one can also interpret AA and BB to be two orbitals lying on a single site. Transforming to momentum space, cn=1N​∑kei​k⋅n​a​ck,c_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k}e^{ik\cdot na}c_{k}, we have

HS​S​H\displaystyle H_{SSH} =∑k(cA,k†cB,k†)​hS​S​H​(k)​(cA,kcB,k),\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\begin{pmatrix}c_{A,k}^{\dagger}&c_{B,k}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}h_{SSH}(k)\begin{pmatrix}c_{A,k}\\ c_{B,k}\end{pmatrix},
hS​S​H​(k)\displaystyle h_{SSH}(k) ≡(0t+λ​e−i​kt+λ​ei​k0)\displaystyle\equiv\begin{pmatrix}0&t+\lambda e^{-ik}\\ t+\lambda e^{ik}&0\end{pmatrix} (2)
=[t+λ​cos⁡(k)]​σ1+λ​sin⁡(k)​σ2.\displaystyle=[t+\lambda\cos(k)]\sigma^{1}+\lambda\sin(k)\sigma^{2}. (3)

As there is no intra-sublattice hopping, there is a chiral symmetry that acts as {hs​s​h​(k),σ3}=0\left\{h_{ssh}(k),\sigma^{3}\right\}=0. Furthermore, there is an inversion symmetry ℐ=σ1\mathcal{I}=\sigma^{1}. Depending on the relative magnitude of tt and λ\lambda, the phases have localized Wannier states on different bonds of the dimerized chain, as shown in Fig. 2.

The critical point occurs at |t|=|λ||t|=|\lambda|. To see this by inspection, we can go to the atomic insulating limit, in which one coupling goes to ∞\infty. In that case, we can access two different atomic insulators, one with bond AA-centered charge and one with bond BB-centered charge. To smoothly deform between these two states would require moving the center of the localized wavefunction away from an inversion center, breaking the inversion symmetry of the system.

As will also be true for the higher dimensional models, there are many invariants which can be used to sharply distinguish the two phases–these include inversion eigenvalues of the Wannier states at high symmetry kk points, the polarization (Zak-Berry phase) [8, 73], and even the presence of zero modes when the model is placed on a finite system with open boundary conditions. However, our focus is not on the characterization of each phase; we will instead focus on the critical theory separating the phases.

From the dispersion ϵ⁡(k)=±t2+λ2+2​t​λ​cos⁡(k)=0\epsilon(k)=\pm\sqrt{t^{2}+\lambda^{2}+2t\lambda\cos(k)}=0, we see the bulk band gap closes at the critical point. Let us focus near the critical point t=λt=\lambda. Writing H⁡(k)=(t+λ​cos⁡k)​σ1+λ​sin⁡k​σ2H(k)=(t+\lambda\cos k)\sigma^{1}+\lambda\sin k\sigma^{2}, near the gap closing at k=πk=\pi, we obtain an effective Dirac theory in the continuum limit,

hS​S​H​(k=π+q)\displaystyle h_{SSH}(k=\pi+q) ≈(t−λ)​σx−λ​q​σy\displaystyle\approx(t-\lambda)\sigma_{x}-\lambda q\sigma_{y}
⟹ℋc​r​i​t\displaystyle\implies\mathcal{H}_{crit} =N​∫d​q2​π​cq†​hS​S​H​(k=π+q)​cq\displaystyle=N\int\frac{dq}{2\pi}c_{q}^{\dagger}h_{SSH}(k=\pi+q)c_{q}
=∫dxΨ†(mσ1−ivσ2∂x)Ψ,\displaystyle=\int dx\;\Psi^{\dagger}(m\sigma^{1}-iv\sigma^{2}\partial_{x})\Psi, (4)

where we have defined the continuum field cq=1N​∫d​x​e−i​q​x​Ψ​(x)c_{q}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\int dx\;e^{-iqx}\Psi(x), mass m=t−λm=t-\lambda, and velocity v=λv=\lambda. Therefore, the critical theory is that of a (1+1)​d(1+1)d massless Dirac fermion.

Once weak, repulsive interactions are added, the critical theory dramatically changes. At the quantum critical point, weak interactions are exactly marginal and lead to a renormalization group (RG) fixed line of (non-Fermi) Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids [26, 64], parametrized by the interaction strength, as shown in Fig. 3. Remarkably, the quasiparticle is lost at the quantum critical point even though both neighboring phases are smoothly connected to band insulators. This is shown in Fig. 4(a-b), where at the critical point, the vanishing of the energy gap is accompanied by a simultaneous vanishing of the quasiparticle residue Z→0Z\rightarrow 0. Furthermore, the spectral function acquires power-law singularities as ω\omega approaches the Fermi level, as opposed to being described by a δ\delta-function in the non-interacting limit. In the original fermion Green’s function, this is reflected in the presence of branch cuts instead simple poles. We note the dramatic change of the spectral function from having δ\delta-function behavior to exhibiting a power law singularity in the presence of interactions is special to one-dimensional Luttinger liquids; from standard finite density Fermi liquid theory, in higher dimensions, weak interactions merely broaden the δ\delta-function peak to a Lorentzian and do not destroy the quasiparticle.

II.2 Bosonic

We now pivot to the bosonic SSH model, in which the critical point is once again described by a Luttinger liquid. We can take

H=∑n=1N(t​bA,n†​bB,n+λ​bB,n†​bA,n+1)+h.c.,H=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(tb_{A,n}^{\dagger}b_{B,n}+\lambda b_{B,n}^{\dagger}b_{A,n+1}\right)+h.c., (5)

where bb is a hard-core boson operator. We set the filling ν=1/2\nu=1/2, or one boson per unit cell. By previous arguments, there will be a phase transition at t=λt=\lambda. To elucidate the ground state properties, we perform a Jordan-Wigner transform,

bi=exp⁡(i​π​∑j=1i−1cj†​cj)​ci,b_{i}=\exp\left(i\pi\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{j}\right)c_{i}, (6)

from which we obtain

H=∑n=1N(t​cA,n†​cB,n+λ​cB,n†​cA,n+1)+h.c.,H=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(tc_{A,n}^{\dagger}c_{B,n}+\lambda c_{B,n}^{\dagger}c_{A,n+1}\right)+h.c., (7)

which is simply the fermionic SSH. To characterize the critical point, we can go near the metallic critical point and re-bosonize using standard methods [54],

cx≈a​(ei​kF​x​ψR​(x)+e−i​kF​x​ψL​(x)),c_{x}\approx\sqrt{a}\left(e^{ik_{F}x}\psi_{R}(x)+e^{-ik_{F}x}\psi_{L}(x)\right), (8)

where we have defined the chiral fermion fields as vertex operators of bosonic fields ϕ\phi and θ\theta

ψR​(x)\displaystyle\psi_{R}(x) ∼12​π​α​ei⁡(ϕ⁡(x)+θ⁡(x)),\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\alpha}}e^{i(\phi(x)+\theta(x))}, (9)

The bosonic fields satisfy the commutation relations

[ϕ⁡(x),θ⁡(x′)]\displaystyle[\phi(x),\theta(x^{\prime})] =i​π2​sgn⁡(x−x′),\displaystyle=i\frac{\pi}{2}\operatorname{sgn}(x-x^{\prime}), (11)
[ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(x′)]\displaystyle[\phi(x),\phi(x^{\prime})] =[θ⁡(x),θ⁡(x′)]=0.\displaystyle=[\theta(x),\theta(x^{\prime})]=0. (12)

As we have ψ†​(x)​ψ​(x)∼1π​∂xϕ⁡(x),\psi^{\dagger}(x)\psi(x)\sim\frac{1}{\pi}\partial_{x}\phi(x), we can write the Jordan Wigner string as

exp⁡(i​π​∫−∞xψ​(y)†​ψ​(y)​𝑑y)=exp⁡(i​kF​x+i​ϕ​(x)).\exp\left(i\pi\int_{-\infty}^{x}\psi(y)^{\dagger}\psi(y)\,dy\right)=\exp\left(ik_{F}x+i\phi(x)\right). (13)

Then, using that the original boson can be written in terms of the vertex operators

b⁡(x)∼12​π​a​(ei​θ​(x)+e2​i​kF​x​ei⁡(2​ϕ​(x)+θ⁡(x))+⋯),b(x)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi a}}\left(e^{i\theta(x)}+e^{2ik_{F}x}e^{i(2\phi(x)+\theta(x))}+\cdots\right), (14)

we can write the boson-boson correlator as

⟨b†​(x,t)​b​(0,0)⟩∼12​π​a​(F0,1​(x,t)+F2,1​(x,t)+⋯).\langle b^{\dagger}(x,t)b(0,0)\rangle\sim\frac{1}{2\pi a}\left(F_{0,1}(x,t)+F_{2,1}(x,t)+\cdots\right). (15)

We have defined

Fa,b​(x,t)=⟨ei⁡(a​ϕ​(x)+b​θ​(x))​e−i⁡(a​ϕ​(0)+b​θ​(0))⟩∼α(a2​K+b2/K)/2(v​t−x−i​α​Θ​(t))(a​K−b/K)2/4​(v​t+x−i​α​Θ​(t))(a​K+b/K)2/4F_{a,b}(x,t)=\langle e^{i(a\phi(x)+b\theta(x))}e^{-i(a\phi(0)+b\theta(0))}\rangle\sim\frac{\alpha^{(a^{2}K+b^{2}/K)/2}}{(vt-x-i\alpha\Theta(t))^{(a\sqrt{K}-b/\sqrt{K})^{2}/4}(vt+x-i\alpha\Theta(t))^{(a\sqrt{K}+b/\sqrt{K})^{2}/4}} (16)

in terms of the Luttinger parameter KK. At large distances and times, one can see algebraic decay of the correlation function, as expected for a Luttinger liquid. Therefore, as in the fermionic case, the bosonic SSH critical point is a gapless, non-Fermi liquid (and CFT).

The critical theory obtained by re-bosonizing after a Jordan-Wigner transformation can be reproduced using a parton decomposition. We can do this by fractionalizing the boson b=d1†​d2b=d_{1}^{\dagger}d_{2} into fermionic partons d1,2d_{1,2}. Performing a mean field decoupling, we can obtain an effective quadratic mean field Hamiltonian,

HS​S​H​(b†,b)=HS​S​H​(d1†,d1)+HS​S​H​(d2†,d2),H_{SSH}(b^{\dagger},b)=H_{SSH}(d_{1}^{\dagger},d_{1})+H_{SSH}(d_{2}^{\dagger},d_{2}), (17)

where each fermionic parton separately realizes an SSH model. Note that the fractionalization of bb introduces an emergent S​U​(2)SU(2) gauge field that is Higgsed to U⁡(1)U(1) by the mean-field decoupling ansatz. To project back into the physical Hilbert space, we impose the constraints d1,i†​d1,i+d2,i†​d2,i=1d_{1,i}^{\dagger}d_{1,i}+d_{2,i}^{\dagger}d_{2,i}=1 and d1,i†​d1,i=d2,i†​d2,i=νB=12d_{1,i}^{\dagger}d_{1,i}=d_{2,i}^{\dagger}d_{2,i}=\nu_{B}=\frac{1}{2} on all sites ii.

The resulting critical theory is Nf=2N_{f}=2 QED2, as there are two Dirac fermions coupled to a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field. The low energy limit of this theory is known [25, 1, 20] and comprises a massive sector in addition to a gapless sector described by the S​U​(2)1SU(2)_{1} Wess-Zumino-Witten theory, a CFT with central charge c=1c=1. Within abelian bosonization, after bosonizing the fermions d1,2d_{1,2} to scalar fields ϕ1,2\phi_{1,2}, ϕ1+ϕ2\phi_{1}+\phi_{2} acquires a mass, while ϕ1−ϕ2\phi_{1}-\phi_{2} remains massless. However, there is no emergent S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry; generically, from microscopic perturbations, there is only a U⁡(1)×U⁡(1)U(1)\times U(1) symmetry, of which a diagonal subgroup is the microscopic charge conservation.

II.3 The Luttinger Liquid Critical Point

From our discussion, we remark that both the fermionic and bosonic SSH models are described under a unified framework by the sine-Gordon theory for the Luttinger liquid,

ℒ=12​π​K​vF​((∂τϕ)2+vF2​(∇ϕ)2)−λ​cos⁡(2​ϕ)+⋯,\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2\pi Kv_{F}}\left((\partial_{\tau}\phi)^{2}+v_{F}^{2}(\nabla\phi)^{2}\right)-\lambda\cos(2\phi)+\cdots, (18)

in which the phase transition is tuned by the sign of λ\lambda and “⋯\cdots” contains higher harmonic operators. Note that from the scaling dimensions Δ⁡[cos⁡(2​n​ϕ)]=K​n2\Delta[\cos(2n\phi)]=Kn^{2}, we obtain the flow

d​λnd​l=(2−K​n2)​λn\dfrac{d\lambda_{n}}{dl}=(2-Kn^{2})\lambda_{n} (19)

under renormalization for couplings λn​cos⁡(2​n​ϕ)\lambda_{n}\cos(2n\phi). If the Luttinger coefficient KK is such that the higher harmonic interactions are irrelevant, then λ=0\lambda=0 is a quantum critical point. For the fermionic SSH model, the electron operator is given by ei⁡(θ±ϕ)e^{i(\theta\pm\phi)}, while for the bosonic SSH model, the boson operator is given by ei​θe^{i\theta}. In both cases, we see that in the presence of interactions (K≠1K\neq 1), there are no quasiparticles at criticality. From Eq. (16), the simple pole in the free limit, K=1K=1, transforms into a branch cut when K≠1K\neq 1.

III Phase Transitions between Atomic Insulators in (2+1)d

To study an obstructed atomic insulator transition in two dimensions, we take the BBH model [6, 5], a representative model of a higher order topological insulator, on the square lattice (Fig. 5). The C4C_{4} symmetric fermionic model realizes a phase transition between an obstructed atomic insulator with a bulk quadrupole moment and a trivial phase. The obstructed phase exhibits mirror-symmetry protected midgap corner modes on an open geometry.

As mentioned earlier, while this wider class of multipole insulators can be characterized based on the nested Wilson loop formalism [6], we will focus only on the critical theories of their phase transitions.

In the fermionic model, the phase transition occurs from Dirac bands touching, leading to a bulk gap closing. The critical theory is that of two massless Dirac fermions, in which short range interactions are irrelevant.

In the bosonic case, fractionalization leads to an emergent QED3 critical point due to the introduction of an emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field. However, the proliferation of (renormalization group relevant) symmetry-allowed monopole operators at the critical point leads the critical point to be fine-tuned and ultimately unstable. Importantly, the symmetry-allowed monopole operators arise from the bipartiteness of the original square lattice [59], which enforces a specific embedding of the UV lattice symmetries into the IR that causes the critical point to be fine-tuned. Consequently, the resulting phase transition is likely first order, and we relegate the details of this model and phase transition to Appendix A.

For the analogous atomic insulators on the triangular lattice, we can realize atomic insulators with C6C_{6} or C3C_{3} rotation symmetry. The first case is realized by a six-orbital model on the triangular lattice. By viewing the orbitals as their own lattice sites, it can be equivalently viewed as a tight binding model on the breathing honeycomb lattice. The second case is realized by a three-orbital model on the triangular lattice, or equivalently, a tight binding model on the breathing kagome lattice [23]. Both lattices are shown in Fig. 6.

From the bipartite nature of the C6C_{6} symmetric model, we expect (and confirm) that the critical point displays similar phenomena to that of the square lattice. The analysis of this model is detailed in Appendix B.

In the C3C_{3} symmetric insulator, however, the lack of bipartiteness allows a possiblity of a stable QED3 critical point and a continuous phase transition. We will explore this model in in the following subsection. We remark that both the C3C_{3} and C6C_{6} symmetric models are primitive generators of rotation symmetric higher order topological crystalline insulators in (2+1)​d(2+1)d [7].

III.1 Fermionic Atomic Insulator on the Breathing Kagome Lattice

On the breathing kagome lattice, we can take hopping parameters as in Fig. 6(b). For λ>t\lambda>t, the insulating phase has Wannier orbitals at the center of each triangle, while for t>λt>\lambda, the phase has Wannier orbitals centered at each hexagonal plaquette. At t=λ=1t=\lambda=1, the resulting state has Dirac cones at the C3C_{3} invariant momenta 𝐊,𝐊′=±(4​π3,0)\mathbf{K},\mathbf{K}^{\prime}=\pm(\frac{4\pi}{3},0). Unlike in the previous models, this occurs at 2/32/3 filling per orbital (22 per unit cell). The relevant symmetries in this case are translation T1,2T_{1,2}, reflection ℛx\mathcal{R}_{x}, time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and C3C_{3} rotation. Near the critical point, the effective Hamiltonian near the Dirac points is (in units of t=1t=1)

He​f​f=\displaystyle H_{eff}= Ψα†​(𝐪)​[q~1​τ1+q~2​τ2+m​μ3​τ3]​Ψα​(𝐪),\displaystyle\Psi_{\alpha}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{q})\left[\tilde{q}^{1}\tau^{1}+\tilde{q}^{2}\tau^{2}+m\mu^{3}\tau^{3}\right]\Psi_{\alpha}(\mathbf{q}), (20)

where m=32​(1−λ)m=\frac{3}{2}(1-\lambda) and q~1,2=32​q1,2\tilde{q}_{1,2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}q_{1,2}. The symmetries forbid any other mass term, so the Dirac theory describes the critical point. The phase diagram is shown in Fig. 7.

III.2 Bosonic Atomic Insulator on the Breathing Kagome Lattice

As in the one-dimensional case, we will take a single species of hardcore boson bb hopping on the lattice, and fractionalize it in terms of fermionic partons d1,2d_{1,2},

b=d1†​d2.b=d_{1}^{\dagger}d_{2}. (21)

This rewriting reproduces the physical Hilbert space given we impose the constraint d1†​d1+d2†​d2=1d_{1}^{\dagger}d_{1}+d_{2}^{\dagger}d_{2}=1 at each site/orbital and set the filling νb=νd2\nu_{b}=\nu_{d_{2}}. We will only impose the constraints on average to arrive at a mean field Hamiltonian

HM​F​(b†,b)=Hi​n​s,t1​(d1†,d1)+Hi​n​s,t2​(d2†,d2),H_{MF}(b^{\dagger},b)=H_{ins,t_{1}}(d_{1}^{\dagger},d_{1})+H_{ins,t_{2}}(d_{2}^{\dagger},d_{2}), (22)

where Hi​n​s,t1H_{ins,t_{1}} is the hopping Hamiltonian for the fermionic insulator on the breathing kagome lattice with coupling t1t_{1}. Note here we have not specified the form of the original bosonic Hamiltonian. As long as it respects all the symmetries of the breathing kagome lattice in addition to time reversal, it can take a fully general form. However, we do assume that there is some parton mean field decoupling such that the mean field state above is realized.

As the spectrum is gapless at 2/32/3 filling per site (or νu​n​i​t​c​e​l​l=2\nu_{unit\;cell}=2), we will fill ν1=1−ν2=13\nu_{1}=1-\nu_{2}=\frac{1}{3}, so the mean field ν1+ν2=1\nu_{1}+\nu_{2}=1 is satisfied. Mapping the bosons to spin operators, this construction realizes a vacuum with a nonzero spin polarization, explicitly breaking the S​U​(2)SU(2) pseudospin symmetry down to U⁡(1)U(1). To ensure the partons simultaneously go critical, we will enforce the time reversal symmetry

𝒯:(d1d2†)→(−d2†d1),\mathcal{T}\;:\;\begin{pmatrix}d_{1}\\ d_{2}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}-d_{2}^{\dagger}\\ d_{1}\end{pmatrix}, (23)

under which bb is invariant. Then, symmetry under 𝒯\mathcal{T} requires that d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} realize the Hamiltonian in Fig. 6(b) with opposite hopping signs. The resulting effective theory is then two copies of Eq. (20) coupled to an emergent U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field aa and can be described by Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3,

ℒE=∑Nf=4Ψ¯(−iγμ(∂μ+iaμ))Ψ+14​e2fμ​ν2+δℒE.\mathcal{L}_{E}=\sum_{N_{f}=4}\overline{\Psi}(-i\gamma^{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}+ia_{\mu}))\Psi+\frac{1}{4e^{2}}f_{\mu\nu}^{2}+\delta\mathcal{L}_{E}. (24)

We have defined γμ=(τ3,−τ2,τ1)\gamma^{\mu}=(\tau^{3},-\tau^{2},\tau^{1}) and Ψ¯=i​Ψ†​τ3\overline{\Psi}=i\Psi^{\dagger}\tau^{3}. The terms in δ​ℒE\delta\mathcal{L}_{E} are needed in order to break the S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} gauge symmetry of the partons down to U​(1)gU(1)_{g}. Concretely, δ​ℒE\delta\mathcal{L}_{E} will contain velocity anisotropies coming from imaginary second-nearest neighbor hoppings (this point is discussed in more detail in Appendix A) and other symmetry-allowed operators.

We remark that the mass in Eq. (20), which has been tuned to zero at the critical point, corresponds to a quantum spin and valley Hall mass in the parton picture, Ψ†​m​τ3​μ3​σ3​Ψ\Psi^{\dagger}m\tau^{3}\mu^{3}\sigma^{3}\Psi. In the IR QED3 theory, the UV lattice symmetries act as

T1:\displaystyle T_{1}\;:\; Ψ→ei​4​π3​μ3​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}\mu^{3}}\Psi, (25)
ℛx:\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{x}\;:\; Ψ→i​τ22​(μ2+3​μ1)​σ3​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\frac{i\tau^{2}}{2}(\mu^{2}+\sqrt{3}\mu^{1})\sigma^{3}\Psi, (26)
C3:\displaystyle C_{3}\;:\; Ψ→ei​π3​τ3​e−i​π3​μ3​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow e^{i\frac{\pi}{3}\tau^{3}}e^{-i\frac{\pi}{3}\mu^{3}}\Psi, (27)
𝒯:\displaystyle\mathcal{T}\;:\; Ψ→τ3​σ2​Ψ∗,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\tau^{3}\sigma^{2}\Psi^{*}, (28)

where we have defined translation T1T_{1} (T2T_{2} acts trivially on Ψ\Psi), reflection ℛx\mathcal{R}_{x} taking x→−xx\rightarrow-x, and C3C_{3} rotation in addition to time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

III.2.1 A Review of the Critical Theory

The quantum field theory in Eq. (24) has been studied extensively, and we will briefly review the relevant details here. We first remark that without δ​ℒE\delta{\mathcal{L}}_{E}, it is believed that Eq. (24) flows to an interacting CFT fixed point [3, 16, 38, 2, 29, 39] for Nf≳4N_{f}\gtrsim 4. Therefore, to analyze the QED3 critical point, one must classify the symmetry-allowed relevant operators contained in δ​ℒE\delta\mathcal{L}_{E}.

As the Dirac fermion ψ\psi is not a local observable, the most important class of local operators are monopole operators ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q}, which insert an integer qq units of U⁡(1)U(1) gauge flux at a spacetime point and describe topologically nontrivial configurations of the gauge field [11, 10]. The monopole operators are charged under the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} conserved current

jμ=12​π​ϵμ​ν​λ​∂νaλ.j^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda}. (29)

In the presence of NfN_{f} Dirac fermions, the monopole operators ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q} must be dressed by fermion zero modes in order to be gauge invariant. The fundamental monopole operators, ℳq=±1\mathcal{M}_{q=\pm 1}, carry unit flux and must have half of its available zero modes filled. As each Dirac fermion contributes a single zero mode in a ±2​π\pm 2\pi flux background, we see there is a total of C⁡(4,2)=6C(4,2)=6 fundamental monopoles.

Schematically, we can write the fundamental monopoles as

ϕ†∼fi†​fj†​ℳ1,\phi^{\dagger}\sim f_{i}^{\dagger}f_{j}^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{1}, (30)

where fi†f_{i}^{\dagger} is the fermion zero mode associated with Ψi\Psi_{i} and ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} creates a single flux quanta in the spacetime without nucleating any zero mode.

All other local operators, such as fermion billinears, can be constructed as composites of the monopole operators (for a more detailed discussion, one can refer to the Appendix of [74]). Therefore, the monopole operators can be viewed as the core building blocks of the theory. Furthermore, from a 1/Nf1/N_{f} expansion, the scaling dimension of the fundamental monopoles ϕ\phi is given by [49, 22]

Δϕ=0.265​Nf−0.0383+𝒪⁡(1/Nf)∼1.02<3,\Delta_{\phi}=0.265N_{f}-0.0383+\mathcal{O}(1/N_{f})\sim 1.02<3, (31)

which is relevant at the QED3 fixed point. Barring fermion billinears, we will assume all other operators (including four fermion terms and higher charge monopoles) in the theory to be irrelevant. These assumptions are within those commonly made for studies of QED3 theories arising from the lattice [29, 74, 75]. Therefore, the fundamental monopoles are the most important operators in determining the ultimate fate of the quantum critical point. Using the methods developed in [59, 60], we will analyze the quantum numbers of monopole operators.

Before proceeding, we note that Eq. (24) will also generically contain velocity anisotropy terms. Refs. [24, 63, 32, 33] have shown a class of these, specified by a valley anisotropy, are irrelevant. Other velocity anisotropies include intravalley contributions. Using a large NfN_{f} expansion, we explicitly show that all velocity anisotropies are irrelevant at the QED3 fixed point in Appendix C.

III.2.2 Monopole Quantum Numbers

We first observe that the QED3 critical point has an enhanced symmetry group compared to that of the atomic insulators on either side of the transition. The QED3 critical point has infrared (IR) time reversal, reflection, charge conjugation, and Lorentz spacetime symmetries, in addition to an IR symmetry,

S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​pℤ2,\dfrac{SO(6)\times U(1)_{top}}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}, (32)

describing the transformation of the monopole operators, the local operators of the theory. The S​O​(6)=S​U​(4)/ℤ2SO(6)=SU(4)/\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry above arises from the S​U​(4)SU(4) fermion flavor symmetry taking ψi→Ui​j​ψj\psi_{i}\rightarrow U_{ij}\psi_{j}. The common ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quotient arises from the fact that, for all local operators, a π\pi rotation in U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} can be compensated by a transformation by the S​O​(6)SO(6) center −𝕀6×6-\mathbb{I}_{6\times 6}. Specifically, the 66 fundamental monopoles transform as a six-dimensional vector under S​O​(6)SO(6).

As the Nf=4N_{f}=4 flavors of Ψi\Psi_{i} naturally split into 22 valleys along with 22 fermionic parton pseudospins, for convenenience, we will define the six monopoles as

ϕ1,2,3†\displaystyle\phi^{\dagger}_{1,2,3} =f†​(i​μ2​μ1,2,3⊗i​σ2)​f†​ℳb​a​r​e,\displaystyle=f^{\dagger}\left(i\mu^{2}\mu^{1,2,3}\otimes i\sigma^{2}\right)f^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{bare}, (33)
ϕ4,5,6†\displaystyle\phi^{\dagger}_{4,5,6} =i​f†​(i​μ2⊗i​σ2​σ1,2,3)​f†​ℳb​a​r​e,\displaystyle=if^{\dagger}\left(i\mu^{2}\otimes i\sigma^{2}\sigma^{1,2,3}\right)f^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{bare}, (34)

where σ\sigma acts on the pseudospin index of the fermionic partons and as defined earlier, μ\mu acts on the valley index. We have set up the monopole basis to respect branching S​O​(6)→S​O​(3)v×S​O​(3)fSO(6)\rightarrow SO(3)_{v}\times SO(3)_{f} for convenience, as the UV symmetries will embed in a way that factors through this product. Note that ϕ1,2,3\phi_{1,2,3} is a singlet under the pseudospin S​O​(3)fSO(3)_{f} while ϕ4,5,6\phi_{4,5,6} is a singlet under the valley S​O​(3)vSO(3)_{v}. On the Dirac fermions, we will choose the IR symmetries to act as

𝒯I​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{IR}\;:\; Ψ→i​γ1​μ2​σ2​Ψ,i→−i,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow i\gamma^{1}\mu^{2}\sigma^{2}\Psi,\quad i\rightarrow-i, (35)
ℛx,I​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{x,IR}\;:\; Ψ→i​γ1​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow i\gamma^{1}\Psi, (36)
𝒞I​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{IR}\;:\; Ψ→i​γ1​μ2​σ2​Ψ∗,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow i\gamma^{1}\mu^{2}\sigma^{2}\Psi^{*}, (37)

where the subscript I​RIR indicates that these are the IR symmetries. We note that the UV symmetries coming from the lattice projective symmetry group, when descending to the IR, will usually involve some combination of the continuum IR symmetries composed with suitable S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p/ℤ2SO(6)\times U(1)_{top}/\mathbb{Z}_{2} transformations, as ff transforms like ψ\psi under the flavor symmetry 22 2 Note that there some ambiguity arising from the common ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quotiented from S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​pSO(6)\times U(1)_{top} global symmetry. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} factor acts as −1-1 on all local operators and can be chosen to be part of S​O​(6)SO(6) or U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top}, depending on convention. This is the same convention that determines whether a symmetry acts as ψ→U​ψ\psi\rightarrow U\psi for U∈S​U​(4)U\in SU(4) or ψ→i​U\psi\rightarrow iU, which differs by a factor of −1-1 on the monopole operators. As the physical symmetry is not convention dependent, the Berry phase should change by π\pi between difference choices of UU or i​UiU. We fix this element of S​U​(4)SU(4) in our calculations by the transformation of the six fermion billinear masses {ψ¯​μi​ψ,ψ¯​σi​ψ}\{\overline{\psi}\mu^{i}\psi,\overline{\psi}\sigma^{i}\psi\}, which also form a vector representation of S​O​(6)SO(6).. For example, 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} reverses the monopole flux and from its action on Ψ\Psi, one can show it must act as

ϕ→±M𝒯I​R​ϕ†,M𝒯I​R=(𝕀3×3−𝕀3×3)\phi\rightarrow\pm M_{\mathcal{T}_{IR}}\phi^{\dagger},\quad M_{\mathcal{T}_{IR}}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{I}_{3\times 3}&\\ &-\mathbb{I}_{3\times 3}\end{pmatrix} (38)

on the six monopoles. The ±\pm factor arises because though the action of any symmetry on Ψ\Psi specifies the S​O​(6)SO(6) transformation factor, the monopole Berry phase coming from the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} must be extracted with other methods. Inherently, the Berry phase is a UV contribution, and intuitively, the phase is accumulated by the monopole moving around the lattice in the parton charge background.

One can also obtain the action of the IR charge conjugation symmetries and reflection. From the S​O​(6)SO(6) action of charge conjugation, we see it must act on the monopoles in the same way as the IR time reversal up to an undetermined phase. As reflection reverses monopole flux, we have that ℛx,I​R\mathcal{R}_{x,IR} acts as ϕ→ϕ†\phi\rightarrow\phi^{\dagger}, up to a uniform phase factor ei​θℛx,I​Re^{i\theta_{\mathcal{R}_{x,IR}}}. We will fix the overall phase of ϕ\phi such that θℛx,I​R=0\theta_{\mathcal{R}_{x,IR}}=0.

To find the Berry phase associated with 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} and 𝒞I​R​ℛx,I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{x,IR}, we follow the analytic argument from [59]. For simplicity, let us assume the UV lattice system has a full S​O​(3)fSO(3)_{f} pseudospin symmetry. First, we introduce a Dirac quantum spin Hall mass ψ¯​σ3​ψ\overline{\psi}\sigma^{3}\psi, which splits the zero mode degeneracy and leaves only the monopole Φ∼ϕ4+i​ϕ5\Phi\sim\phi_{4}+i\phi_{5} that transforms as SzS_{z} to be gapless. As the spin Hall mass preserves the IR time reversal, the time reversal Berry phase for the original system can be calculated in the presence of this spin Hall mass. Then, the nontriviality of the spin Hall state ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topological insulator [36] is manifested through the monopole acquiring a minus sign under the Kramers time reversal, Φ→−Φ†\Phi\rightarrow-\Phi^{\dagger}. This can be seen by examining the edge theory of the spin Hall insulating state and identifying the monopole with a particular tunneling operator on the edge. The same arguments apply to 𝒞I​R​ℛx,I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{x,IR}, leading to

𝒯I​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{IR}\;:\; (ϕ1,2,3ϕ4,5,6)→(ϕ1,2,3†−ϕ4,5,6†),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}\\ \phi_{4,5,6}\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}^{\dagger}\\ -\phi_{4,5,6}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix},
𝒞I​R​ℛx,I​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{x,IR}\;:\; (ϕ1,2,3ϕ4,5,6)→(ϕ1,2,3−ϕ4,5,6).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}\\ \phi_{4,5,6}\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}\\ -\phi_{4,5,6}\end{pmatrix}. (39)

Note that while the above argument does not discriminate between the valley and spin S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetries, the same argument does not apply when we choose to a condense a valley Hall mass ψ¯​μ3​ψ\overline{\psi}\mu^{3}\psi. This is because the resulting valley Hall state does not admit a physical edge to the vacuum due to a parity anomaly, manifested as a mixed anomaly between S​O​(3)fSO(3)_{f} and S​O​(3)vSO(3)_{v}. Such an anomaly does not affect the spin Hall state because the continuous valley symmetry is not present in the microscopic system and instead is only emergent in the IR. Note that, as we will discuss shortly, the above arguments can be generalized to the case of the breathing kagome atomic insulator, which only has a microscopic U⁡(1)⊂S​O​(3)fU(1)\subset SO(3)_{f} psuedospin symmetry.

We are now ready to analyze the monopole quantum numbers for the C3C_{3} symmetry atomic insulator. To begin, we will list the final transformation properties of the monopoles in Table 1.

To arrive at the transformations, we first note that the translations T1,2T_{1,2} should act with trivial U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} Berry phase. This can be shown algebraically using that the critical point has an emergent C6C_{6} about each hexagonal plaquette. From the relation T1​C6​T2=T2​C6T_{1}C_{6}T_{2}=T_{2}C_{6} and the fact that ϕ4,5,6\phi_{4,5,6} transform with only a phase under T1,2T_{1,2} and C6C_{6}, one can see that the Berry phase for T1T_{1} must vanish. The Berry phase for T2T_{2} must also vanish by the relation C6​T1=T2​C6C_{6}T_{1}=T_{2}C_{6}. To find the Berry phase for C3C_{3}, we can use numerical methods [60], putting the system on a torus and threading 2​π2\pi flux uniformly. Filling the appropriate zero modes (which will have a finite size gap), we calculate the quantum numbers of the resulting many body state to confirm the valley singlet monopoles have zero C3C_{3} angular momentum, as well as zero lattice momentum.

Lastly, we must determine the Berry phases for the discrete symmetries. As before, we set ℛx\mathcal{R}_{x} to have trivial Berry phase as this corresponds to fixing an overall phase shift of all monopoles. To determine the Berry phase for 𝒯\mathcal{T}, it will be useful to recall the IR QED3 symmetries defined in Eq. (35). We see that 𝒯\mathcal{T} acts exactly as the continuum 𝒞I​R​𝒯I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{T}_{IR} composed with a spin flip symmetry i​σ2i\sigma^{2} and a Lorentz rotation that does not affect the monopoles. As ℛI​R\mathcal{R}_{IR} acts as ϕ†→ϕ\phi^{\dagger}\rightarrow\phi, determining the Berry phase associated with 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} and 𝒞I​R​ℛI​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{IR} will determine the Berry phase of 𝒯\mathcal{T}. To do this, we will condense a quantum spin Hall mass ψ¯​σ3​ψ\overline{\psi}\sigma_{3}\psi as before, leading to a nontrivial topological insulator. Even though we do not have microscopic S​U​(2)SU(2) pseudospin symmetry, there is still a residual U⁡(1)U(1) rotation about the pseudospin polarization axis corresponding to the U​(1)bU(1)_{b} boson conservation symmetry, which is unbroken by the spin hall mass. Consequently, the resulting state is still a nontrivial ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topological insulator. The previous arguments then still apply, and the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} nontriviality is reflected in the phase of the spin triplet monopole acquiring a minus sign under time reversal. The final transformations of the IR discrete symmetries are identical to the cases in which full S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is present,

𝒯I​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{IR}\;:\; (ϕ1,2,3ϕ4,5,6)→(ϕ1,2,3†−ϕ4,5,6†),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}\\ \phi_{4,5,6}\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}^{\dagger}\\ -\phi_{4,5,6}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}, (40)
𝒞I​R​ℛI​R:\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{IR}\;:\; (ϕ1,2,3ϕ4,5,6)→(ϕ1,2,3−ϕ4,5,6).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}\\ \phi_{4,5,6}\end{pmatrix}\rightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1,2,3}\\ -\phi_{4,5,6}\end{pmatrix}. (41)

From the above, the monopoles under 𝒯\mathcal{T} must have the transformation as outlined in Table. 1.

III.2.3 The bosonic critical point

The results of Table. 1, along with U​(1)bU(1)_{b} boson conservation symmetry, forbid the proliferation of any trivial monopole operator, as the only singlet monpoles under the lattice and discrete symmetries are either non-Hermitian (such as ϕ3†−ϕ3\phi_{3}^{\dagger}-\phi_{3}) or break U​(1)bU(1)_{b} (such as Im⁡[ϕ4]\operatorname{Im}[\phi_{4}]).

The next most relevant operators are the fermion billinear operators, which we have tuned to zero to reach the critical point. As discussed earlier, other singlet operators, which include excited charge 11 monopole operators, higher charge monopoles, and operators which transform as symmetric two-index tensors of S​O​(6)SO(6), are likely irrelevant by analytic and numeric computations, or they must be assumed irrelevant if Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 is found to be stable in any lattice gauge model (more detailed discussion in [74]). Therefore, we find that the critical point between the two trivial insulating phases on the breathing kagome lattice is a natural candidate for realizing the QED3 CFT. This CFT is stable and unfine-tuned as there is only a single relevant perturbation (the fermion mass) tuning the transition.

The insulators on each side of the transition can be viewed as QED3 perturbed by an S​U​(4)SU(4) adjoint mass, which breaks the IR global symmetry to (S​O​(4)×S​O​(2))/ℤ2(SO(4)\times SO(2))/\mathbb{Z}_{2}. However, note that the appearance of a trivial single-charge monopole is forbidden by the UV symmetries. While it is possible that the adjoint mass can lead to monopole proliferation which precipitates spontaneous symmetry breaking [60], we assume instead that the adjoint mass drives proliferation of higher charge, UV singlet monopoles, which further breaks the IR global symmetry to the UV symmetry of the lattice insulator. These higher charge monopoles, which drive confinement, are in the class of UV singlet operators that are irrelevant at the critical point, but become relevant once we deform away from criticality. The schematic scaling of the fermion (parton) gap, mm, and the photon gap Δp​h\Delta_{ph} away from the critical point is shown in Fig. 8. In particular, we note that as the photon is gapped by higher charge, dangerously irrelevant monopoles, Δp​h\Delta_{ph} will be parametrically smaller than the fermion gap mm.

IV Anomaly Matching Conditions

In this section, we confirm the quantum numbers of the monopoles in the three models we have analyzed is indeed consistent with what is expected from the lattice Lieb-Shultz-Mattis-Oshikawa-Hastings (LSMOH) constraints [40, 45, 28, 15, 47, 34, 17, 35, 62]. Applying the tools developed in [76, 72], this illustrates that the critical theories discussed and the symmetry transformations of the monopoles, including for the unstable multicritical points on the bipartite lattices, are consistent with what can be emergent from a local bosonic lattice Hamiltonian like the ones we described, providing a nontrivial check on our results.

We will briefly describe the general framework for LSMOH anomaly matching. To begin, we view the critical QED3 field theory as emergent from the lattice at the gapless critical point. The local operators in the QED3 theory are then coarse grained version of lattice operators, matched by their symmetry properties. Formally, the correspondence between the UV and IR symmetries is determined by a group homomorphism from the UV symmetry group GU​V{G}_{UV} to the IR symmetry group GI​R=S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​pℤ2G_{IR}=\frac{SO(6)\times U(1)_{top}}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}} (in addition to discrete symmetries),

φ:GU​V→GI​R.\varphi\;:\;G_{UV}\rightarrow G_{IR}. (42)

However, it turns out that not every symmetry embedding φ\varphi is physically consistent. In particular, if the IR theory contains a ’t Hooft anomaly η⁡[GI​R]\eta[G_{IR}], that anomaly must pull back under φ\varphi to the anomaly of the UV,

η⁡[GU​V]=φ∗​η​[GI​R].\eta[G_{UV}]=\varphi^{*}\eta[G_{IR}]. (43)

As η⁡[GU​V]\eta[G_{UV}] is determined by lattice LSMOH theorems, anomaly matching provides a constraint on how φ\varphi can act. In Eq. (43), both η⁡[GU​V]\eta[G_{UV}] and φ∗​η​[GI​R]\varphi^{*}\eta[G_{IR}] are elements in H4​(GU​V,U​(1)T)H^{4}(G_{UV},U(1)_{T}), where U​(1)TU(1)_{T} indicates time reversal acts as complex conjugation. While Eq. (43) is a necessary condition for a theory to be “emergeable” from the lattice, it is expected that anomaly matching is also a sufficient condition.

The most simple LSMOH theorem applies to a lattice with an odd number of spin-1/21/2 degree of freedoms in each translation invariant unit cell. Upon coupling the system to background gauge fields of the S​O​(3)SO(3) spin symmetry and the T1,2T_{1,2} translation symmetries, the resulting theory is anomalous, with a bulk SPT anomaly

η⁡[GU​V]=exp⁡(i​π​∫X4w2S​O​(3)∪x∪y),\eta[G_{UV}]=\exp\left(i\pi\int_{X_{4}}w_{2}^{SO(3)}\cup x\cup y\right), (44)

where x,y∈H1​(X4,ℤ2)x,y\in H^{1}(X_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{2}) are the translation gauge fields. There are similar anomalies that activate when an odd number of spin-1/21/2 moments located on reflection or rotation axes. Furthermore, there are LSMOH constraints for time reversal when the spin-1/21/2 object is also a Kramers doublet.

All the models we consider are particularly simple, in that there is no lattice LSMOH anomaly. Therefore, all of the IR anomalies should pullback to zero and the LHS of Eq. (43) is trivial. However, as the RHS of Eq. (43) describes the nontrivial IR anomaly, the matching condition still enforces nontrivial relations for the symmetry embedding φ\varphi. To explicitly show this, we first write down the IR anomaly for Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 by coupling S​O​(6)SO(6) and U​(1)t​o​p=S​O​(2)U(1)_{top}=SO(2) gauge fields, considering it as a Stiefel liquid [76]. The resulting nonlinear sigma model has the same symmetries and anomalies as QED3.

We will perform the proper anomaly matching procedure in Appendix D. In particular, simplification occurs because of the absence of UV lattice LSM anomalies in the critical points we consider.

Note that anomaly matching does not make any statement about the dynamics of the IR theory. In particular, for the IR theory to be stable, all relevant perturbations must not be singlets under GU​VG_{UV}. For the case of bipartite lattices, while anomaly matching shows QED3 is an emergeable CFT at the critical point, our earlier analysis shows that it is dynamically unstable due to the presence of RG relevant GU​VG_{UV} singlet monopoles.

V Outlook

In this paper, we have examined how a certain class of phase transitions between trivial bosonic atomic insulating states can realize exotic critical points through fractionalization. Beginning with the SSH chain as a warm-up example, we showed how both fermionic and bosonic systems lead naturally to a Luttinger liquid at criticality, in which the underlying particles do not have integrity as quasiparticles. Elevating to two dimensions via the BBH model on the square lattice, a bosonic parton construction that fractionalizes the boson into two fermions produces an Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 description of the putative critical point. Crucially, however, lattice symmetries control the monopole content of the low-energy theory–on bipartite lattices, a symmetry-allowed monopole operator exists and destabilizes the QED3 fixed point. In the presence of the symmetry-allowed Dirac mass that tunes the transition, the combination of these relevant perturbations leads to an inherently multicritical structure, and we argued the transition is generically first-order. By contrast, on tripartite lattices such as the C3C_{3}-symmetric breathing kagome, all monopoles can be symmetry-forbidden and a genuine, stable QED3 critical point is possible.

A unifying message of our analysis is that the fate of “trivial-to-trivial” insulating transitions depends sensitively on the UV to IR embedding of the lattice symmetries and not simply on band topology. The observation that Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 on bipartite lattices admits a deformation to Nf=2N_{f}=2 QCD3 gives a robust route to identifying at least one monopole singlet under all microscopic symmetries, enforcing an instability of the QED3 critical point in those settings. Conversely, when symmetry forbids all relevant monopoles, the emergent, critical gauge theory description is unfine-tuned. We corroborated these conclusions with LSMOH anomaly matching for lattice bosons; every critical theory we discussed, including those that are dynamically unstable, matches the appropriate anomalies and is thus realizable in microscopic lattice models.

Note that our methods can be straightforwardly extended to higher dimensions [41, 42], such as for the pyrochlore [23] or cubic lattice obstructed atomic insulator. However, due to the tendency toward deconfinement in higher dimensions, we expect a conformal critical point to be less common. As QED4 coupled to fermions is free in the IR and behaves like a pure gauge theory, one may need to employ parton constructions that involve a nonabelian gauge group. In the setting of more general gauge groups, such as S​U​(Nc)SU(N_{c}), there is a conformal window of NfN_{f} for which there exists a conformal fixed point (the Banks-Zak fixed point [14, 4]). For S​U​(2)SU(2) fundamental fermions, we must have approximately 8≲Nf≲118\lesssim N_{f}\lesssim 11, which is harder to realize in lattice models unless there are multiple degenerate bands. However, these general theories could be an interesting avenue of exploration as (3+1)​d(3+1)d gauge theories realize a large class of “unnecessary” quantum critical points [9], which may emerge as low energy descriptions in both fermionic and bosonic lattice insulators.

Moreover, in this paper we have only considered a particular type of transition: namely, those arising from Dirac fermions acquiring a mass. More general transitions, such quadratic band touchings, will generically be described by some Lifshitz-type theory with gauge fields. Looking forward, it would be fruitful to explore aspects of fractionalization and criticality in different settings such as in different dimensions and with more general internal symmetries. While such critical points could be analyzed within a parton mean-field theory as we have done, we expect many classes of critical points between atomic insulators to be beyond parton constructions and perhaps only describable intrinsically, such as in terms of anomalies and without reference to an explicit Lagrangian or Hamiltonian.

Lastly, whether a specific microscopic Hamiltonian realizes the QED3 critical point or is preempted by a weakly first-order transition or intermediate phase is a dynamical question. Our analysis has identified universal properties and the conditions under which QED3 criticality is allowed, and as the models explored in this paper are relatively simple, there is hope that the unusual critical behavior, at least in the non-finetuned case of the breathing kagome lattice, can be probed in the future through both numerical simulations and laboratory experiments.

Appendix A C4C_{4}-symmetric atomic insulator on the square: The BBH Model

A.1 The Fermionic BBH Model

The BBH model [6, 5] consists of four orbitals describing spinless fermions on a square lattice. There are dimerized hopping amplitudes corresponding to intra- and inter-site coupling. Furthermore, π\pi flux is threaded through each plaquette as shown in Fig. 5. The hopping Hamiltonian is given by,

This theory has been extensively studied due to its emergence in graphene, and short-range interactions are irrelevant at the critical point. A.3 Monopole quantum numbers

For convenience, we will calculate the symmetry properties of the monopole operators in the original BBH model with no particle-hole symmetry breaking perturbations as such perturbations do not affect the monopole quantum numbers. We adopt the same basis of monopole operators that was outlined in the main text,

ϕ1,2,3†\displaystyle\phi^{\dagger}_{1,2,3} =f†​(i​μ2​μ1,2,3⊗i​σ2)​f†​ℳb​a​r​e,\displaystyle=f^{\dagger}\left(i\mu^{2}\mu^{1,2,3}\otimes i\sigma^{2}\right)f^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{bare}, (65)
ϕ4,5,6†\displaystyle\phi^{\dagger}_{4,5,6} =i​f†​(i​μ2⊗i​σ2​σ1,2,3)​f†​ℳb​a​r​e\displaystyle=if^{\dagger}\left(i\mu^{2}\otimes i\sigma^{2}\sigma^{1,2,3}\right)f^{\dagger}\mathcal{M}_{bare} (66)

Recall the low energy theory, Eq. (64), is that of Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 on the square lattice, with all Dirac nodes located at momentum 𝐌=(π,π)\mathbf{M}=(\pi,\pi). In the Dirac basis, the physical symmetries act as

T1,2:\displaystyle T_{1,2}\;:\; Ψ→−Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow-\Psi, (67)
ℛx:\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{x}\;:\; Ψ→τ2​μ1​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\tau^{2}\mu^{1}\Psi, (68)
C4:\displaystyle C_{4}\;:\; Ψ→i2​ei​π4​τ3​(μ2+μ3)​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}e^{i\frac{\pi}{4}\tau^{3}}(\mu^{2}+\mu^{3})\Psi, (69)
𝒯:\displaystyle\mathcal{T}\;:\; Ψ→−i​τ2​μ2​σ2​Ψ.\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow-i\tau^{2}\mu^{2}\sigma^{2}\Psi. (70)

Furthermore, we will define a charge conjugation 𝒞\mathcal{C} symmetry in the parton model that acts 𝒞\mathcal{C} in Eq. (52) in addition to a spin flip on the partons,

𝒞:Ψ→i​τ1​μ3​σ2​Ψ∗.\mathcal{C}\;:\;\Psi\rightarrow i\tau^{1}\mu^{3}\sigma^{2}\Psi^{*}. (71)

Up to a U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} phase, the above symmetries determine the symmetry transformations of the monopoles.

Now to fully constrain the monopole transformations, especially the Berry phases of the UV lattice symmetry transformations, we will again borrow from [59]. Note that due to the particle-hole symmetry inherent in the bipartite square lattice, the hopping Hamiltonian can be adiabatically tuned to a point with an enhanced S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} gauge symmetry, as in the case of taking the diagonal hopping terms λ2→0\lambda_{2}\rightarrow 0. A particle-hole symmetry is then restored at this point. For example, for a site iai_{a} on the aa sublattice, there is a symmetry

dα,ia→(−1)a​i​σα​β2​dβ,ia†,d_{\alpha,i_{a}}\rightarrow(-1)^{a}i\sigma^{2}_{\alpha\beta}d^{\dagger}_{\beta,i_{a}}, (72)

where (dα,ia,i​σα​β2​dβ,ia†)(d_{\alpha,i_{a}},i\sigma^{2}_{\alpha\beta}d^{\dagger}_{\beta,i_{a}}) forms an S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} fundamental. The resulting critical point is then described Nf=2N_{f}=2 QCD3. At low energies, QED3 can recovered if S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} is Higgsed.

Equivalently, we can view the Higgsed QCD3 as a mid-IR theory in which S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} has been Higgsed down to U⁡(1)U(1), while the particle-hole symmetry still survives as a global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry. In either case, there turns out to be a unique embedding of implementation of the lattice UV symmetries into the QCD3, such that the QED3 theory that will contain a trivial (symmetry-allowed) spin-singlet monopole. Specifically, the S​O​(5)SO(5) flavor symmetry of the Nf=2N_{f}=2 QCD3 theory will embed into the S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p/ℤ2SO(6)\times U(1)_{top}/\mathbb{Z}_{2} of QED3 in such a way that five of the six monopoles transform as an S​O​(5)SO(5) vector, while the remaining singlet monopole will be trivial under all symmetries. Because it is a singlet in the mid-IR theory, this singlet monopole will remain a singlet in the IR QED3 theory, as the process of flowing the IR by adding charge conjugation symmetry breaking and other irrelevant perturbations will not change any monopole quantum numbers. We have thus shown the presence of one trivial, symmetry-allowed monopole operator.

From another point of view, the map of symmetry groups

GU​V→GQ​E​D3G_{UV}\rightarrow G_{QED_{3}} (73)

must factor through the mid-IR QCD3 theory, such that we have a map,

GU​V→GQ​C​D3→GQ​E​D3.G_{UV}\rightarrow G_{QCD_{3}}\rightarrow G_{QED_{3}}. (74)

Then the embedding GQ​C​D3→GQ​E​D3G_{QCD_{3}}\rightarrow G_{QED_{3}} guarantees a trivial monopole, from which we conclude GU​V→GQ​E​D3G_{UV}\rightarrow G_{QED_{3}} must also lead to a trivial monopole. This feature is present whenever the U⁡(1)U(1) gauge theory that can be adiabatically tuned to have S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} gauge symmetry, as in the case generically for parton models on bipartite lattices.

We can now apply this knowledge. To begin, we see that all the monopoles are trivial under translation. Under C4C_{4}, we have ϕ†→ei​θC4​OC4​ϕ†\phi^{\dagger}\rightarrow e^{i\theta_{C_{4}}}O_{C_{4}}\phi^{\dagger}, where

OC4=(−111111).O_{C_{4}}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&&&&&\\ &&1&&&\\ &1&&&&\\ &&&1&&\\ &&&&1&\\ &&&&&1\end{pmatrix}. (75)

However, from the fact that there exists a singlet monopole, we know that the U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} phase should be chosen so that OC4O_{C_{4}} takes the form

OC4​(1U),O_{C_{4}}\begin{pmatrix}1&\\ &U\end{pmatrix}, (76)

for U∈S​O​(5)U\in SO(5). Therefore, θC4=π\theta_{C_{4}}=\pi. The time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} acts exactly the bare time reversal 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR} defined in Eq. (39). Note we have used here that the S​O​(3)fSO(3)_{f} pseudospin rotation symmetry must be part of the S​O​(5)SO(5), so that the S​O​(5)SO(5) singlet monopole must be a spin singlet (so one of ϕ1,2,3\phi_{1,2,3}).

For the symmetries of charge conjugation and reflection, we observe that the operator 𝒞​ℛx\mathcal{C}\mathcal{R}_{x} can be viewed as a combination of 𝒞I​R​ℛx,I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}\mathcal{R}_{x,IR} and a Lorentz rotation that does not affect the monopoles, which are Lorentz scalars. The overall phase of 𝒞​ℛx\mathcal{C}\mathcal{R}_{x} can be fixed by noting that (𝒞​ℛx)2=1(\mathcal{C}\mathcal{R}_{x})^{2}=1 on the fermions. From the arguments in [59], (𝒞​ℛx)2=1(\mathcal{C}\mathcal{R}_{x})^{2}=1 is another manifestation of the nontriviality of the spin Hall insulator, in which the spin triplet monopoles must be odd under 𝒞​ℛx\mathcal{CR}_{x}. Therefore, the (spin triplet) monopoles in this system must also transform the same way, which uniquely determines the combined action 𝒞​ℛx\mathcal{C}\mathcal{R}_{x}. Note that one of 𝒞\mathcal{C} and ℛx\mathcal{R}_{x} can be defined with an arbitrary overall U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} phase, as this amounts to shifting all the monopoles by an overall phase. However, their relative actions are physically relevant and determined by the arguments above. The symmetry transformations are gathered in Table 2.

We see straightforwardly that the real part of ϕ1\phi_{1}, Re⁡[ϕ1]∼ϕ1†+ϕ\operatorname{Re}[\phi_{1}]\sim\phi_{1}^{\dagger}+\phi is a trivial monopole. However, we note one surprise: Im⁡[ϕ2−ϕ3]∼i⁡(ϕ2†−ϕ3†−ϕ2+ϕ3)\operatorname{Im}[\phi_{2}-\phi_{3}]\sim i(\phi_{2}^{\dagger}-\phi_{3}^{\dagger}-\phi_{2}+\phi_{3})is also symmetry allowed! More generally, the insertion of either of these operators into the Lagrangian is allowed by symmetry, and as these operators are strongly relevant at the critical point, we then do not expect the Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 CFT to be the ultimate fate of the critical point. Instead, the presence of these two monopoles, ⟨Re⁡[ϕ1]⟩,⟨Im⁡[ϕ2−ϕ3]⟩≠0\langle\operatorname{Re}[\phi_{1}]\rangle,\langle\operatorname{Im}[\phi_{2}-\phi_{3}]\rangle\neq 0, will destabilize the QED3 theory and destroy the conformal fixed point, leading to what is most likely a first-order transition.

A.3.1 Multicriticality

Note the resulting phase, between two different atomic insulators on the square lattice, is multicritical, as it requires the fine tuning of three independent (RG relevant) parameters. Recall that to reach the QED3 critical point, one must already tune the mass i​Ψ¯​(μ2+μ3)​Ψi\overline{\Psi}(\mu_{2}+\mu_{3})\Psi from Eq. (55) to zero. This mass term is equivalent to the monopole-antimonopole pair,

Im⁡[ϕ1†​(ϕ2−ϕ3)].\operatorname{Im}[\phi_{1}^{\dagger}(\phi_{2}-\phi_{3})]. (77)

There are also other allowed monopole-antimonopole terms such as ϕ1†​ϕ1\phi_{1}^{\dagger}\phi_{1}, and these terms have scaling dimension ∼2.38\sim 2.38 from large NfN_{f}. However, as mentioned earlier, we will assume that they are irrelevant as is done in numerical calculations, due to the fact that any lattice realization of QED3 will contain singlets of this form [29, 74, 75].

From the case of the BBH model, we observe that in all transitions between bosonic atomic insulators in which the critical point is accessed through tuning a fermion billinear mass i​Ψ¯​M​Ψi\overline{\Psi}M\Psi to zero, the existence of a single trivial monopole ϕt​r​i​v\phi_{triv} may imply the existence of an additional one. This is because in addition to the trivial monopole ϕt​r​i​v\phi_{triv}, the tuning mass i​Ψ¯​M​Ψi\overline{\Psi}M\Psi is also an allowed relevant operator and is equivalent to a monopole-antimonopole pair ∼Im⁡[ϕM1†​ϕM2]\sim\operatorname{Im}[\phi_{M_{1}}^{\dagger}\phi_{M_{2}}] for some {M1,M2}\{M_{1},M_{2}\}. These operators can be identified because a zero flux monopole-antimonopole composite transforms as the antisymmetric two indexed tensor representation of S​O​(6)SO(6) (𝟏𝟓⊂𝟔⊗𝟔\mathbf{15}\subset\mathbf{6}\otimes\mathbf{6}), which is exactly the adjoint of S​U​(4)SU(4). Then, one can see that in the case that ϕt​r​i​v\phi_{triv} coincides with one of ϕM1,2\phi_{M_{1,2}}, then ϕM2,1\phi_{M_{2,1}} will also be symmetry allowed. Therefore, in cases in which there is one trivial monopole (as is generically the case for the square and honeycomb lattices), we would expect such critical points to be highly multicritical and unstable as in the case we just examined.

The resulting multicritical point will presumably be driven to strong coupling by the two monopole operators, and will have a reduced symmetry

S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​pℤ2→S​O​(4)×S​O​(2),\dfrac{SO(6)\times U(1)_{top}}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}\rightarrow SO(4)\times SO(2), (78)

where the S​O​(2)SO(2) rotates among the two singlet monopoles. The remaining state hosts an S​O​(4)SO(4) symmetry anomaly, so the theory cannot flow to an S​O​(4)SO(4) symmetric gapped state. To see this, one can imagine adding the monopoles one at a time. Adding the first monopole breaks S​O​(6)→S​O​(5)SO(6)\rightarrow SO(5), leading to the anomaly for Nf=2N_{f}=2 QCD3, with bulk partition function on a 4-manifold X4X_{4}

Z⁡[AS​O​(5),X4]=exp⁡(π​i​∫X4w4​[AS​O​(5)]),Z[A^{SO(5)},X_{4}]=\exp\left(\pi i\int_{X_{4}}w_{4}[A^{SO(5)}]\right), (79)

for w4​[AS​O​(5)]∈H4​(X4,ℤ2)w_{4}[A^{SO(5)}]\in H^{4}(X_{4},\mathbb{Z}_{2}), corresponding to a discrete θ\theta-angle for the background S​O​(5)SO(5) gauge field AS​O​(5)A^{SO(5)}. Proliferating the second trivial monopole will restrict our symmetry to an S​O​(4)SO(4) subgroup of S​O​(5)SO(5). Decomposing S​O​(4)=(S​U​(2)L×S​U​(2)R)/ℤ2SO(4)=(SU(2)_{L}\times SU(2)_{R})/\mathbb{Z}_{2}, the anomaly becomes [65]

Z⁡[AS​U​(2)L,AS​U​(2)R,X4]=exp⁡(i2​C​SS​U​(2),X4​[AS​U​(2)L]−i2​C​SS​U​(2),X4​[AS​U​(2)R]),Z[A^{SU(2)_{L}},A^{SU(2)_{R}},X_{4}]=\exp\left(\frac{i}{2}CS_{SU(2),X_{4}}[A^{SU(2)_{L}}]-\frac{i}{2}CS_{SU(2),X_{4}}[A^{SU(2)_{R}}]\right), (80)

where C​SS​U​(2),X4​[A]=14​π​∫X4trf​u​n​d⁡F∧FCS_{SU(2),X_{4}}[A]=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{X_{4}}\operatorname{tr}_{fund}F\wedge F is the extension of the Chern-Simons term into X4X_{4}. This anomaly corresponds to opposite discrete θ\theta-angles for S​U​(2)LSU(2)_{L} and S​U​(2)R⊂S​O​(4)SU(2)_{R}\subset SO(4), and with time reversal, the θ\theta angles do not flow. Most importantly, the resulting theory cannot be a trivial, symmetric gapped phase. There is a possibility that in the presence of two singlet monopoles, the critical point flows to a conformal fixed point distinct from QED3. Note that despite the ’t Hooft anomaly, the state enjoys symmetry-enforced gaplessness [66, 67, 58, 65, 19, 18], in which the anomaly precludes even a gapped symmetric topologically ordered state. The argument is similar to the one in [21]. Because S​U​(2)SU(2) is simply-connected, it cannot have a non-trivial action on a (2+1)​d(2+1)d TQFT; that is, S​U​(2)SU(2) cannot carry any non-trivial anomaly. However, the θ\theta terms imply a non-trivial anomaly for an S​U​(2)SU(2) subgroup of S​O​(4)SO(4). Instead, a topologically ordered state must break the S​O​(4)SO(4) or time reversal (in which case the θ\theta can flow to be trivial).

Therefore, as in the case posited for a single monopole [74, 75], it is more plausible that the final fate of the theory could be some ordered state that spontaneously breaks the remaining S​O​(4)SO(4) symmetry. In either case, the highly multicritical nature of the critical point leads us to conclude the transition we have constructed is likely first-order.

We observe that in the above picture, the two insulating phases of the BBH model near the critical point correspond to turning on a suitable S​U​(4)SU(4) adjoint mass for ψ\psi while not proliferating any of the two singlet monopoles. This gaps out the fermion matter fields, leaving a pure gauge theory in the IR. Upon turning on the mass, the degeneracy of the six monopoles will be lifted, and there will be one unique gapless monopole in the IR, specifically ϕ1±i​ϕ2−ϕ32\phi_{1}\pm i\frac{\phi_{2}-\phi_{3}}{\sqrt{2}}. This monopole will spontaneously proliferate as it is also a singlet under the UV symmetries, leading to confinement of the resulting gauge theory. The resulting state (in addition to the discrete symmetries of 𝒞I​R\mathcal{C}_{IR}, 𝒯I​R\mathcal{T}_{IR}, and ℛI​R\mathcal{R}_{IR}) will have an S​O​(4)×S​O​(2)/ℤ2SO(4)\times SO(2)/\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry, where S​O​(2)SO(2) acts as a combination of U​(1)t​o​pU(1)_{top} and rotating among the singlet monopoles while S​O​(4)SO(4) rotates the other four and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} acts as before. A simple ordered state is allowed, and consequently, there is no anomaly even in the IR. However, we still expect the IR symmetry to completely break the global symmetry to the symmetry of the UV square lattice space group. This is because in the presence of the adjoint mass, the UV singlet terms allowed in δ​ℒE\delta{\mathcal{L}}_{E} that were irrelevant at the critical point (such as higher strength monopoles) will become relevant and will completely break the IR continuous vector symmetries into discrete subgroups corresponding to the UV lattice symmetries. We remark that the activation of an adjoint mass in QED3 is also a possible mechanism by which conventional Landau symmetry-breaking orders can originate from the a Dirac spin liquid phase or critical point, also described by QED3 [60]. However, our case is distinct in that the adjoint mass is not a mechanism for symmetry breaking as it is already a singlet under all UV symmetries.

Appendix B C6C_{6}-symmetric atomic insulator on the breathing honeycomb lattice

B.1 Fermionic

We begin with a hopping model on the breathing honeycomb lattice with real couplings as shown in Fig. 6(a). The spectrum is gapped at half-filling, with two Dirac cones at 𝐤=𝚪\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{\Gamma}. For λ>t\lambda>t, the phase hosts Wannier orbitals at the hexagonal plaquette centers, while for t>λt>\lambda, the Wannier centers are located at the hexagonal plaquette edges. At quantum critical point t=λt=\lambda, the spectrum becomes gapless. The model’s symmetries include translation T1,2T_{1,2}, reflection ℛx\mathcal{R}_{x}, time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T}, particle-hole symmetry 𝒞\mathcal{C} (from the bipartite nature of the lattice), and C6C_{6} rotation about a plaquette. Near the critical point, we obtain an effective Hamiltonian near the Dirac points

He​f​f=Ψα†​(𝐪)​[q~1​τ1+q~2​τ2+m⁡(3​μ2−μ3)​τ3]​Ψα​(𝐪),H_{eff}=\Psi_{\alpha}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{q})\left[\tilde{q}_{1}\tau^{1}+\tilde{q}_{2}\tau^{2}+m(\sqrt{3}\mu^{2}-\mu^{3})\tau^{3}\right]\Psi_{\alpha}(\mathbf{q}), (81)

where q~1=−q1+3​q2\tilde{q}_{1}=-q_{1}+\sqrt{3}q_{2} and q~2=−3​q1−q2\tilde{q}_{2}=-\sqrt{3}q_{1}-q_{2}. As previously, τ\tau acts on the spinor/Lorentz index and μ\mu acts on the valley index α\alpha. We have defined the mass m=1−λ2m=\frac{1-\lambda}{2} in units of t=1t=1. By the microscopic lattice symmetries, no other mass terms are allowed. Therefore, the Dirac theory is a non-finetuned critical point between the two diferent fermionic trivial insulating phases, as before.

B.2 Bosonic

In the bosonic case, we repeat the steps done before, fractionalizing the hardcore boson on the lattice into fermionic partons b=d1†​d2b=d_{1}^{\dagger}d_{2}, having the partons each realize the Hamiltonian in Fig. 10, and half-filling each fermionic parton.

The resulting theory is again that of Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3,

where δ​ℒE\delta\mathcal{L}_{E} contains irrelevant contributions and velocity anisotropy terms that Higgs the S​U​(2)gSU(2)_{g} gauge symmetry to d1,2d_{1,2} down to U⁡(1)U(1). Repeating the steps done for the square lattice, we will project the action of the lattice symmetries onto the Dirac fermions to find

T1,2:\displaystyle T_{1,2}\;:\; Ψ→Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\Psi, (83)
ℛx:\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{x}\;:\; Ψ→12​(−τ2​μ1+3​τ1​μ1)​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}(-\tau^{2}\mu^{1}+\sqrt{3}\tau^{1}\mu^{1})\Psi, (84)
C6:\displaystyle C_{6}\;:\; Ψ→14​(i​3​τ0​μ3−τ3​μ3−i​3​τ0​μ2+3​τ3​μ2)​Ψ,\displaystyle\Psi\rightarrow\frac{1}{4}(i\sqrt{3}\tau^{0}\mu^{3}-\tau^{3}\mu^{3}-i3\tau^{0}\mu^{2}+\sqrt{3}\tau^{3}\mu^{2})\Psi, (85)

Importantly, the breathing honeycomb lattice is also bipartite and will therefore host at least one trivial monopole. Using the same methods as earlier, we find the transformation of all monopole operators, tabulated in Table 3. We comment that the Berry phase for C6C_{6} is given by θC6=π\theta_{C_{6}}=\pi, and the action of charge conjugation and reflection can again be determined by seeing that (𝒞​ℛx)2=1(\mathcal{CR}_{x})^{2}=1, which means the spin triplet monopoles will be odd under 𝒞​ℛx\mathcal{CR}_{x}.

B.3 Multicriticality

As found in the case of the square lattice, there are two trivial monopoles: Re⁡[ϕ1]\operatorname{Re}[\phi_{1}] and Im⁡[3​ϕ2/3+ϕ3]\operatorname{Im}[\sqrt{3}\phi_{2}/3+\phi_{3}]. From the bipartite nature of the lattice, there is an adiabatic deformation to an effective QCD3 theory that necessitates the existence of the trivial monopole Re⁡[ϕ1]\operatorname{Re}[\phi_{1}]. Then, the combination of Re⁡[ϕ1]\operatorname{Re}[\phi_{1}] and the tuning mass leads to the existence of a second trivial monopole Im⁡[3​ϕ2/3+ϕ3]\operatorname{Im}[\sqrt{3}\phi_{2}/3+\phi_{3}]. Again, such a structure of singlet monopoles is expected as the tuning mass is exactly the composite monopole operator Im⁡[ϕ1​(3​ϕ2/3+ϕ3)]\operatorname{Im}\left[\phi_{1}(\sqrt{3}\phi_{2}/3+\phi_{3})\right].

Compared with the BBH square lattice insulator, an essentially identical analysis applies here, from which we conclude that the quantum critical point is actually multicritical, leading to what is likely a first-order transition between the two atomic insulating phases. As before, aside from some more exotic possibilities, after the monopoles have proliferated, the final fate of the critical point is likely a state that spontaneously breaks the residual S​O​(4)SO(4) IR symmetry.
