C.3 Renormalization

Collecting the above results and restoring the valley index (ν)(\nu) in Γν​ρσ\Gamma^{\sigma}_{\nu\rho}, we obtain the vertex function

Γ=\displaystyle\Gamma= (1−8+24​ξ3​π2​Nf​ln⁡kΛ)​k̸+∑νμν​∑ρ≠σΓν​ρσ​kσ​γρ+(Γν​ρσ​56−120​ξ15​π2​Nf+Γρν​σ​325​π2​Nf)​kσ​γρ​ln⁡kΛ\displaystyle\left(1-\dfrac{8+24\xi}{3\pi^{2}N_{f}}\ln\frac{k}{\Lambda}\right)\not{k}+\sum_{\nu}\mu^{\nu}\sum_{\rho\neq\sigma}\Gamma^{\sigma}_{\nu\rho}k_{\sigma}\gamma^{\rho}+\left(\Gamma^{\sigma}_{\nu\rho}\dfrac{56-120\xi}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}+\Gamma_{\rho}^{\nu\sigma}\dfrac{32}{5\pi^{2}N_{f}}\right)k_{\sigma}\gamma^{\rho}\ln\frac{k}{\Lambda}
∑νμν​∑ρΓρν​ρ​kρ​γρ+(Γν​ρρ​88−120​ξ15​π2​Nf−∑λ≠ρΓν​λλ​6415​π2​Nf)​kρ​γρ​ln⁡kΛ\displaystyle\sum_{\nu}\mu^{\nu}\sum_{\rho}\Gamma_{\rho}^{\nu\rho}k_{\rho}\gamma^{\rho}+\left(\Gamma^{\rho}_{\nu\rho}\dfrac{88-120\xi}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}-\sum_{\lambda\neq\rho}\Gamma_{\nu\lambda}^{\lambda}\dfrac{64}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}\right)k_{\rho}\gamma^{\rho}\ln\frac{k}{\Lambda} (117)

The renormalization two point vertex is related to the above bare through a field renormalization ZΨZ_{\Psi}, such that ΓR=ZΨ​Γ\Gamma_{R}=Z_{\Psi}\Gamma. For our renormalization condition, we demand that at a momentum scale pp, ΓR​(p)\Gamma_{R}(p) has the form p̸+∑νμν​∑ρ,σ(Γν​ρσ)R​kσ​γρ\not{p}+\sum_{\nu}\mu^{\nu}\sum_{\rho,\sigma}(\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\sigma})_{R}k_{\sigma}\gamma^{\rho}, which gives us

ZΨ=1+8+24​ξ3​π2​Nf​ln⁡pΛ,Z_{\Psi}=1+\frac{8+24\xi}{3\pi^{2}N_{f}}\ln\frac{p}{\Lambda}, (118)

from which we can derive the renormalized velocities:

  • •

    For ρ=σ\rho=\sigma,

    (Γν​ρρ)R​(p)=Γν​ρρ​(1+8+24​ξ3​π2​Nf​ln⁡pΛ)+(Γν​ρρ​88−120​ξ15​π2​Nf−∑λ≠ρΓν​λλ​6415​π2​Nf)​ln⁡pΛ,(\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\rho})_{R}(p)=\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\rho}\left(1+\frac{8+24\xi}{3\pi^{2}N_{f}}\ln\frac{p}{\Lambda}\right)+\left(\Gamma^{\rho}_{\nu\rho}\dfrac{88-120\xi}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}-\sum_{\lambda\neq\rho}\Gamma_{\nu\lambda}^{\lambda}\dfrac{64}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}\right)\ln\frac{p}{\Lambda}, (119)

    from which allowing p∼e−lp\sim e^{-l} yields the beta function

    dd​l​(Γν​ρρ)R=−12815​π2​Nf​Γν​ρρ+6415​π2​Nf​∑λ≠ρΓν​λλ.\dfrac{d}{dl}(\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\rho})_{R}=-\frac{128}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\rho}+\frac{64}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}\sum_{\lambda\neq\rho}\Gamma_{\nu\lambda}^{\lambda}. (120)
  • •

    For ρ≠σ\rho\neq\sigma,

    (Γν​σρ)R​(p)=Γν​ρσ​(1+8+24​ξ3​π2​Nf​ln⁡pΛ)+(Γν​ρσ​56−120​ξ15​π2​Nf+Γρν​σ​325​π2​Nf)​ln⁡pΛ,(\Gamma_{\nu\sigma}^{\rho})_{R}(p)=\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\sigma}\left(1+\frac{8+24\xi}{3\pi^{2}N_{f}}\ln\frac{p}{\Lambda}\right)+\left(\Gamma^{\sigma}_{\nu\rho}\dfrac{56-120\xi}{15\pi^{2}N_{f}}+\Gamma_{\rho}^{\nu\sigma}\dfrac{32}{5\pi^{2}N_{f}}\right)\ln\frac{p}{\Lambda}, (121)

    which gives

    dd​l​(Γν​σρ)R=−325​π2​Nf​Γν​σρ−325​π2​Nf​Γν​ρσ.\dfrac{d}{dl}(\Gamma_{\nu\sigma}^{\rho})_{R}=-\frac{32}{5\pi^{2}N_{f}}\Gamma_{\nu\sigma}^{\rho}-\frac{32}{5\pi^{2}N_{f}}\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\sigma}. (122)

Therefore, we see that all perturbations of the form dd​l​(Γν​ρρ)R\dfrac{d}{dl}(\Gamma_{\nu\rho}^{\rho})_{R} are irrelevant. Under the above renormalization scheme, the first bullet point yields the flow eigenvectors described by couplings −i​Γ1​Ψ¯​μ​(γ1​D1−γ2​D2)​ψ-i\Gamma_{1}\overline{\Psi}\mu(\gamma^{1}D_{1}-\gamma^{2}D_{2})\psi with

βΓ1=−645​π2​Nf​Γ1,\beta_{\Gamma_{1}}=-\frac{64}{5\pi^{2}N_{f}}\Gamma_{1}, (123)

and −i​Γ2​Ψ¯​μ​(γμ​Dμ)​Ψ-i\Gamma_{2}\overline{\Psi}\mu(\gamma^{\mu}D_{\mu})\Psi, which is marginal to one loop in 1Nf\frac{1}{N_{f}}. The second bullet point gives us the couplings −i​Γ3​Ψ¯​μ​(γ1​D2+γ2​D1)​Ψ-i\Gamma_{3}\overline{\Psi}\mu(\gamma^{1}D_{2}+\gamma^{2}D_{1})\Psi with

βΓ3=−645​π2​Nf​Γ3,\beta_{\Gamma_{3}}=-\frac{64}{5\pi^{2}N_{f}}\Gamma_{3}, (124)

and −i​Γ4​Ψ¯​μ​(γ1​D2−γ2​D1)​Ψ-i\Gamma_{4}\overline{\Psi}\mu(\gamma^{1}D_{2}-\gamma^{2}D_{1})\Psi, which is marginal. Furthermore, as desired, our renormalization group analysis is fully gauge invariant as there is no dependence on the gauge fixing parameter ξ\xi.

The above suggests that the QED3 fixed point is not destabilized by velocity anisotropies, except for the two marginal anisotropic perturbations above. However, we will demonstrate that the two marginal operators Γ2\Gamma_{2} and Γ4\Gamma_{4} are redundant operators, and therefore, do not affect the conformal fixed point. In more detail, a redundant operator is any operator in the action that can be removed by a continuous definition of the fields [69],

Ψl​(x)→Ψl​(x)+ϵ​Fl​(Ψ⁡(x),∂μΨ⁡(x),⋯).\Psi^{l}(x)\rightarrow\Psi^{l}(x)+\epsilon F^{l}(\Psi(x),\partial_{\mu}\Psi(x),\cdots). (125)

Such operators do not affect any observables of the theory. Furthermore, the field redefinition in Eq. (125) changes the Lagrangian as

δ​ℒ=ϵ​∑lδ​ℒδ​Ψl​Fl​(Ψ⁡(x),∂μΨ⁡(x),⋯).\delta\mathcal{L}=\epsilon\sum_{l}\dfrac{\delta\mathcal{L}}{\delta\Psi_{l}}F^{l}(\Psi(x),\partial_{\mu}\Psi(x),\cdots). (126)

Thus, a redundant operator is equivalently one that vanishes on the equations of motion, δ​ℒδ​Ψ=0\frac{\delta\mathcal{L}}{\delta\Psi}=0. Strictly speaking, the renormalization group behavior of a redundant operator is scheme dependent and not universal [68]. In our renormalization group flow, both Γ2\Gamma_{2} and Γ4\Gamma_{4} are marginal as they arise from a constant rescaling (or reparametrization) of Ψ\Psi at the fixed point. Specifically, Γ2\Gamma_{2} can be eliminated from the action at the fixed point theory by redefining Ψ→Ψ−Γ22​μ​Ψ\Psi\rightarrow{\Psi}-\frac{\Gamma_{2}}{2}\mu{\Psi}, followed by a field renormalization, while Γ4\Gamma_{4} can be eliminated by redefining Ψ→Ψ+i​Γ42​μ​γ0​Ψ{\Psi}\rightarrow\Psi+i\frac{\Gamma_{4}}{2}\mu\gamma^{0}\Psi and then rescaling the time coordinate.

Appendix D LSM Anomaly Matching

We follow the approach outlined in [72]. Recall that from Eq. (43) in the main text we must match the anomalies as elements of the group cohomology H4​(GU​V,U​(1)T)H^{4}(G_{UV},U(1)_{T}). The U⁡(1)U(1) coefficients complicate the process, but for the groups we are considering, H4​(GU​V,U​(1)T)H^{4}(G_{UV},U(1)_{T}) is just a product of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} factors. Then, it is much simpler to calculate the IR and UV anomalies as elements of H4​(GU​V,ℤ2)H^{4}(G_{UV},\mathbb{Z}_{2}). This equates to viewing

η⁡[GU​V/I​R]=exp⁡(i​π​Ω​[GU​V/I​R]),\eta[G_{UV/IR}]=\exp\left(i\pi\Omega[G_{UV/IR}]\right), (127)

where Ω⁡[GU​V/I​R]∈H4​(GU​V/I​R,ℤ2)\Omega[G_{UV/IR}]\in H^{4}(G_{UV/IR},\mathbb{Z}_{2}). The operation exp(iπ∙)\exp(i\pi\bullet) can be considered as an inclusion ℤ2→U⁡(1)\mathbb{Z}_{2}\rightarrow U(1).

However, in practice, we will use an analogous relation to Eq. (43) but instead consider the UV anomaly and the pullback of the IR anomaly as elements of H5​(GU​V,ℤ2)H^{5}(G_{UV},\mathbb{Z}_{2}). Though this matching occurs in one higher dimension, it is much simpler than confirming Eq. (43). The reason is that the induced map on cohomology from exp(iπ∙)\exp(i\pi\bullet) (for which we will use the same notation),

exp(iπ∙):H4(GU​V,ℤ2)→H4(GU​V,U(1)T){\exp(i\pi\bullet)}\;:\;H^{4}(G_{UV},\mathbb{Z}_{2})\rightarrow H^{4}(G_{UV},U(1)_{T}) (128)

is not injective, so that confirming the anomaly matching and pullback condition in H4​(GU​V,ℤ2)H^{4}(G_{UV},\mathbb{Z}_{2}) is not equivalent to showing that η⁡[GU​V]=φ∗​η​[GI​R]∈H4​(GU​V,U​(1)T)\eta[G_{UV}]=\varphi^{*}\eta[G_{IR}]\in H^{4}(G_{UV},U(1)_{T}). The anomaly matching in H4​(GU​V,ℤ2)H^{4}(G_{UV},\mathbb{Z}_{2}) is a sufficient but not necessary condition. In other words, one can have

(η⁡[GU​V])=φ∗​(η⁡[GI​R])(\eta[G_{UV}])=\varphi^{*}(\eta[G_{IR}]) (129)

but

Ω⁡[GU​V]≠φ∗​(Ω⁡[GI​R]).\Omega[G_{UV}]\neq\varphi^{*}(\Omega[G_{IR}]). (130)

The correct matching condition that is equivalent to Eq. (43) is

𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GU​V])=φ∗​𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GI​R]).\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[G_{UV}])=\varphi^{*}\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[G_{IR}]). (131)

where the operation 𝒮​𝒬1\mathcal{SQ}^{1} is a composition of maps 𝒮𝒬1=ρ2∘β∘exp(iπ∙)\mathcal{SQ}^{1}=\rho_{2}\circ\beta\circ{\exp(i\pi\bullet)}. We have defined ρ2\rho_{2} to be reduction ℤ→ℤ2\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{2}, β\beta as the Bockstein homomorphism taking Hn​(G,U​(1)T)→Hn+1​(G,ℤ)H^{n}(G,U(1)_{T})\rightarrow H^{n+1}(G,\mathbb{Z}), and exp(iπ∙){\exp(i\pi\bullet)} as the map in cohomology,

exp(iπ∙):H4(GU​V,ℤ2)→H4(GU​V,U(1)T).{\exp(i\pi\bullet)}\;:\;H^{4}(G_{UV},\mathbb{Z}_{2})\rightarrow H^{4}(G_{UV},U(1)_{T}). (132)

In particular exp(iπ∙)\exp(i\pi\bullet) maps the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} valued class Ω⁡[G]\Omega[G] into the U⁡(1)U(1) valued anomaly η⁡[G]\eta[G]. More details can be found in [72].

D.1 The form of η\eta and Ω\Omega for GU​V/I​RG_{UV/IR}

To begin, we note that in all of our UV models, there is no lattice LSMOH theorem that applies, as we have trivial bosons, which are integer S​O​(3)SO(3) spin and Kramers singlets, occupying each unit cell and high symmetry point. Note in the kagome atomic insulator, the UV symmetry is no longer S​O​(3)×ℤ2T×Gl​a​t​t​i​c​eSO(3)\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{T}\times G_{lattice} but S​O​(2)×ℤ2T×Gl​a​t​t​i​c​eSO(2)\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{T}\times G_{lattice} due to the spin polarization of the vacuum in our parton description. However, in all cases, we have that η⁡[GU​V]\eta[G_{UV}] and Ω⁡[GU​V]\Omega[G_{UV}] are trivial.

Now in the IR, we have Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3 with GI​R=S​O​(6)×U​(1)t​o​p/ℤ2G_{IR}={SO(6)\times U(1)_{top}}/{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}. However, there is not yet a known form of the anomaly GI​RG_{IR} in terms of characteristic classes for the GI​RG_{IR} anomaly for Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3. Instead, we will consider a slightly simplified description of the anomaly by coupling S​O​(6)SO(6) and U​(1)t​o​p=S​O​(2)U(1)_{top}=SO(2) gauge fields, considering the QED3 CFT as a Stiefel liquid [76], which provides a dual description of the theory in terms of a nonlinear sigma model. Allowing time reversal, we must then consider an O​(6)T×O​(2)TO(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T} gauge bundle, where the subscript TT indicates that improper rotations in O⁡(2)O(2) or O⁡(6)O(6) must be composed with a spacetime orientation reversal symmetry. Mathematically, this constrains

w1T​M+w1O⁡(6)+w1O⁡(2)=0(mod2),w_{1}^{TM}+w_{1}^{O(6)}+w_{1}^{O(2)}=0\pmod{2}, (133)

in terms of the Stiefel-Whitney classes of the tangent, O⁡(6)O(6), and O⁡(2)O(2) bundles. The ’t Hooft anomaly is then characterized by an SPT bulk, [76]

exp⁡[i​π​(w4O⁡(6)+w2O⁡(6)​(w2O⁡(2)+(w1O⁡(2))2)+((w2O⁡(2))2+w2O⁡(2)​(w1O⁡(2))2+(w1O⁡(2))4))].\displaystyle\exp\left[i\pi\left(w_{4}^{O(6)}+w_{2}^{O(6)}\left(w_{2}^{O(2)}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}\right)+\left((w_{2}^{O(2)})^{2}+w_{2}^{O(2)}(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{4}\right)\right)\right]. (134)

Note that the above symmetry group O​(6)T×O​(2)TO(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T} does not consider the discrete ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quotient and is therefore larger than the faithful IR symmetry group O​(6)T×O​(2)T/ℤ2{O(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T}}/{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}. Consequently, the above anomaly is a coarser description of the actual anomaly of Nf=4N_{f}=4 QED3. In a different physical system, the above anomaly could still be accurate if there are additional gapped, trivial vector degrees of freedom in the IR. In any case, we will use the enlarged symmetry as only then is there a (known) expression for the anomaly that allows us to examine the anomaly matching explicitly. Using the englarged G~I​R=O​(6)T×O​(2)T\tilde{G}_{IR}=O(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T}, we have

η⁡[G~I​R]\displaystyle\eta[\tilde{G}_{IR}] =exp⁡[i​π​(w4O⁡(6)+w2O⁡(6)​(w2O⁡(2)+(w1O⁡(2))2)+((w2O⁡(2))2+w2O⁡(2)​(w1O⁡(2))2+(w1O⁡(2))4))]\displaystyle=\exp\left[i\pi\left(w_{4}^{O(6)}+w_{2}^{O(6)}\left(w_{2}^{O(2)}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}\right)+\left((w_{2}^{O(2)})^{2}+w_{2}^{O(2)}(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{4}\right)\right)\right]
⟹Ω⁡[G~I​R]\displaystyle\implies\Omega[\tilde{G}_{IR}] =w4O⁡(6)+w2O⁡(6)​(w2O⁡(2)+(w1O⁡(2))2)+((w2O⁡(2))2+w2O⁡(2)​(w1O⁡(2))2+(w1O⁡(2))4).\displaystyle=w_{4}^{O(6)}+w_{2}^{O(6)}\left(w_{2}^{O(2)}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}\right)+\left((w_{2}^{O(2)})^{2}+w_{2}^{O(2)}(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{4}\right). (135)

For here onwards and the calculation of the pullback, we will drop the tilde and consider GI​R=O​(6)T×O​(2)TG_{IR}=O(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T} for simplicity. Mathematically, this is equivalent to taking the UV to IR embedding φ\varphi, factorizing into two parts

φ:GU​V→O​(6)T×O​(2)T→O​(6)T×O​(2)Tℤ2,\varphi\;:\;G_{UV}\rightarrow O(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T}\rightarrow\frac{O(6)_{T}\times O(2)_{T}}{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}, (136)

and considering the pullback of only the first part of the embedding.

Lastly, we note that under the operator 𝒮​𝒬1\mathcal{SQ}^{1}, the IR anomaly takes the form

𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GI​R])=w5O⁡(6)+w4O⁡(6)​w1O⁡(2)+w3O⁡(6)​(w2O⁡(2)+(w1O⁡(2))2)+\displaystyle\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[{G}_{IR}])=w_{5}^{O(6)}+w_{4}^{O(6)}w_{1}^{O(2)}+w_{3}^{O(6)}\left(w_{2}^{O(2)}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}\right)+ w2O⁡(6)​(w1O⁡(2))3+((w2O⁡(2))2​w1O⁡(2)+(w1O⁡(2))5)+\displaystyle w_{2}^{O(6)}(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{3}+\left((w_{2}^{O(2)})^{2}w_{1}^{O(2)}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{5}\right)+
w1O⁡(6)​((w2O⁡(2))2+w2O⁡(2)​(w1O⁡(2))2+(w1O⁡(2))4).\displaystyle w_{1}^{O(6)}\left((w_{2}^{O(2)})^{2}+w_{2}^{O(2)}(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{2}+(w_{1}^{O(2)})^{4}\right). (137)

Then, Eq. (131) amounts to checking

φ∗​𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GI​R])=0\varphi^{*}\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[{G}_{IR}])=0 (138)

for the three critical points considered in our paper.

D.2 Calculating the Pullbacks

We begin by performing anomaly matching for the square lattice critical point. We note for the square lattice (and all the cases we consider), it is clear from Table 2 that the symmetry O​(6)T=O​(3)v×O​(3)fO(6)_{T}=O(3)_{v}\times O(3)_{f} factorizes into O​(3)v,fO(3)_{v,f} blocks for the valley and pseudospin symmetries acting on the monopole operators. Repeatedly applying the Whitney product formula allows us to calculate the pullbacks of each block, in terms of cohomology classes of GU​V=p​4​m×O​(3)TG_{UV}=p4m\times O(3)_{T}

φ∗​(w1O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(3)_{v}}) =0\displaystyle=0 (139)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{v}}) =r2\displaystyle=r^{2} (140)
φ∗​(w3O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{3}^{O(3)_{v}}) =0\displaystyle=0 (141)
φ∗​(w1O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(3)_{f}}) =t\displaystyle=t (142)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{f}}) =w2O​(3)T\displaystyle=w_{2}^{O(3)_{T}} (143)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{f}}) =w3O​(3)T.\displaystyle=w_{3}^{O(3)_{T}}. (144)

We have defined t∈H1​(ℤ2T,ℤ2)t\in H^{1}(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{T},\mathbb{Z}_{2}) as the gauge field corresponding time-reversal symmetry and r∈H1​(p​4​m,ℤ2)r\in H^{1}(p4m,\mathbb{Z}_{2}) as the reflection gauge field. Note that O​(3)TO(3)_{T} represents the S​O​(3)×ℤ2TSO(3)\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{T} transformation. As ℤ2T\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{T} acts as minus one in the S​O​(3)SO(3) block, we have w3O​(3)T=w3S​O​(3)+t​w2S​O​(3)+t3w_{3}^{O(3)_{T}}=w_{3}^{SO(3)}+tw_{2}^{SO(3)}+t^{3}. Assembling the above, one can find

φ∗​(w1O⁡(6))\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(6)}) =t,\displaystyle=t, (145)
φ∗​(w2O⁡(6))\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(6)}) =r2+w2O​(3)T,\displaystyle=r^{2}+w_{2}^{O(3)_{T}}, (146)
φ∗​(w3O⁡(6))\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{3}^{O(6)}) =t​r2+w3O​(3)T,\displaystyle=tr^{2}+w_{3}^{O(3)_{T}}, (147)
φ∗​(w4O⁡(6))\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{4}^{O(6)}) =r2​w2O​(3)T,\displaystyle=r^{2}w_{2}^{O(3)_{T}}, (148)
φ∗​(w5O⁡(6))\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{5}^{O(6)}) =r2​w3O​(3)T.\displaystyle=r^{2}w_{3}^{O(3)_{T}}. (149)

Moreover, we can find the O⁡(2)O(2) contributions

φ∗​(w1O⁡(2))=r,φ∗​(w2O⁡(2))=0.\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(2)})=r,\quad\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(2)})=0. (150)

Combining the above and substituting into Eq. (137), we indeed obtain Eq. (131), φ∗​𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GI​R])=0\varphi^{*}\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[{G}_{IR}])=0.

For the breathing honeycomb lattice, we introduce an additional gauge field cc for C2C_{2} rotation, from which we find from Table 3

φ∗​(w1O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(3)_{v}}) =0\displaystyle=0 (151)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{v}}) =r2+c2+r​c\displaystyle=r^{2}+c^{2}+rc (152)
φ∗​(w3O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{3}^{O(3)_{v}}) =c​r​(r+c)\displaystyle=cr(r+c) (153)
φ∗​(w1O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(3)_{f}}) =t\displaystyle=t (154)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{f}}) =w2O​(3)T\displaystyle=w_{2}^{O(3)_{T}} (155)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{f}}) =w3O​(3)T.\displaystyle=w_{3}^{O(3)_{T}}. (156)

The O⁡(2)O(2) contributions are

φ∗​(w1O⁡(2))=r,φ∗​(w2O⁡(2))=c2+c​r,\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(2)})=r,\quad\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(2)})=c^{2}+cr, (157)

from which we can confirm φ∗​𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GI​R])=0\varphi^{*}\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[{G}_{IR}])=0.

For the breathing kagome lattice, we will use the transformations from Table 1,

φ∗​(w1O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(3)_{v}}) =0\displaystyle=0 (158)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{v}}) =r2\displaystyle=r^{2} (159)
φ∗​(w3O​(3)v)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{3}^{O(3)_{v}}) =0\displaystyle=0 (160)
φ∗​(w1O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(3)_{f}}) =0\displaystyle=0 (161)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{f}}) =w2O​(2)T+t2\displaystyle=w_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}+t^{2} (162)
φ∗​(w2O​(3)f)\displaystyle\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(3)_{f}}) =t​w2O​(2)T,\displaystyle=tw_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}, (163)

where here, O​(2)TO(2)_{T} refers to the UV spin rotation symmetry that acts on the monopoles ϕ4,5\phi_{4,5}. Note that from the embedding of the UV symmetries, we have w2O​(2)T=w2S​O​(2)+r2+r​tw_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}=w_{2}^{SO(2)}+r^{2}+rt. The O⁡(2)O(2) contributions are

φ∗​(w1O⁡(2))=r+t,φ∗​(w2O⁡(2))=0,\varphi^{*}(w_{1}^{O(2)})=r+t,\quad\varphi^{*}(w_{2}^{O(2)})=0, (164)

from which we can find

φ∗​𝒮​𝒬1​(Ω⁡[GI​R])=w2O​(2)T​r​t2+r2​t3+t3​r2\varphi^{*}\mathcal{SQ}^{1}(\Omega[{G}_{IR}])=w_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}rt^{2}+r^{2}t^{3}+t^{3}r^{2} (165)

We can simplify the above using the Steenrod square as the first term vanishes,

w2O​(2)T​r​t2=S​q1​(w2O​(2)T​t2)+w2O​(2)T​t3=0,\displaystyle w_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}rt^{2}=Sq^{1}(w_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}t^{2})+w_{2}^{O(2)_{T}}t^{3}=0, (166)

as for an O⁡(2)O(2) bundle, S​q1​(w2)=w1​w2Sq^{1}(w_{2})=w_{1}w_{2}. The second and third terms on the RHS of Eq. (165) also vanish, as

r2​t3+r3​t2=S​q1​(r2​t2)+r3​t2+r3​t2=0.r^{2}t^{3}+r^{3}t^{2}=Sq^{1}(r^{2}t^{2})+r^{3}t^{2}+r^{3}t^{2}=0. (167)

Therefore, as desired, all of the critical points we have considered are consistent with anomaly matching.
